blocks.x: Sampleson Backgrounds is a new soundscape-creation tool. Combining words and ideas on a canvas produces an ever-shifting, cinematic ambience.

At its core is semantic audio search, matching words and concepts against a curated library of over 22,000 audio cells and 11,000 local embeddings. Users build soundscapes by dragging keywords like strings, rain, bass, and thunder onto the canvas and blending them.
It runs entirely on your own computer, with no cloud processing or subscription tokens. It comes as a standalone app and a plugin, ready for use directly in music production and sound design work.
It is available now as a standalone app for macOS and Windows and as a VST3/AU plugin. The launch price is $39 (regular price $59).

IMPF and IMPEL, representing independent music publishers, have put out principles the industry should follow when licensing to generative AI platforms. At the top is one "non-negotiable" principle: songs must be properly valued, and unless there is some other clear reason, they must be paid at least as much as recordings.

When AI companies use existing music for training and services, this calls for pricing the royalties for the two rights embedded in a single track — the recording (master) right and the song (composition) right — at nearly the same level. In streaming, recordings have always been paid far more than songs. The two groups say that, having disputed streaming's imbalance for years, they see generative AI as a chance to build a fairer framework, and that a model which gives songs a small share while directing most of the revenue to masters is "unacceptable."

They stress that songs, lyrics, and melodies sit at the center of AI music products, from training through prompting, generation, output, and commercialization. They also said licensing scope must be specific and must not inadvertently create a pathway to broader future uses.

They also called for transparency. Rights holders should know what is being licensed, how works are used and how attribution is handled, what deductions apply, and how revenue is calculated and distributed. Payments for past use, training, output, and future use should be clearly separated and treated fairly.

As majors push their AI partners to prioritize remix and mashup tools that use existing tracks, at least two separate revenue streams arise: payment for training and payment for use of output. Since the two streams may be split differently, the principles become more useful. IMPF chair Annette Barrett said, "Songs are at the heart of all of this and must be protected."

UK-based Absolute Label Services is opening its AI-driven music operating system, Anthology, to the entire independent music industry. It's a white-label business management platform, and its first customers are Cherry Red Records and Blue Raincoat Music, part of Reservoir Media.

At Absolute, a "music OS" isn't a single feature—it's the company's term for software that spans a rights company's data and operations as a whole. Anthology links together global digital and physical distribution, neighboring-rights registration, marketing, financial reporting, inventory and supplier management, and invoicing. Running through all of it is Absolute's own LLM, "Ant."

Simon Wills, who leads Anthology, said concerns about "what AI means for creativity, copyright and the value of human-made music are legitimate," but added that "AI is much bigger than generating music." He said the focus was on helping people rather than replacing them—letting AI watch over data around the clock to catch anomalies, royalty issues and business opportunities that are easy to miss.

He explained that Ant is rooted in decades of music-industry knowledge built up by Absolute, and that customers retain full data sovereignty. The company spent several years and several million pounds building the system, and has been using it internally since July 2024.

Cherry Red's Matt Bristow said he's had to enter data separately into 15 platforms for a single release, and that with around 30 releases a month, the system will save significant time every month. Wills said music companies can't keep negotiating with the likes of Google, Apple, Meta and Spotify using PDFs and spreadsheets, and stressed that music companies need their own technological capability.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit upheld a lower-court ruling that AI companies' copying of copyrighted works to build training data is not fair use. The court sided with Thomson Reuters, which owns the legal search service Westlaw. Its opponent was Ross Intelligence, a startup that built a competing search tool using Westlaw's case summaries (headnotes) and has since shut down.

The Recording Industry Association of America (RIAA) and the National Music Publishers' Association (NMPA) filed a joint brief arguing that training AI models on copyrighted works to build a competing service "cannot be fair use." The 32-page ruling remains under seal. Once unsealed, it will become binding precedent for district courts in the circuit.

The two groups cited a filing in which Suno said it trained its model on "nearly all of the quality music files available on the internet." They also cited figures Deezer disclosed showing it was receiving more than 50,000 fully AI-generated tracks a day in November 2025, a number that grew to nearly 90,000 a day by June of this year. They pointed to deals between UMG and Warner with Stability AI and Udio, and between Kobalt and ElevenLabs, as evidence that a real market for training-data licensing exists.

Still, the ruling doesn't resolve the fair-use question in the Suno and Udio cases. Ross was a tool for finding existing case law, not generative AI. Judge Stephanos Bibas, who issued the lower-court ruling, drew that same line in his 2025 decision, writing that it dealt "only with non-generative AI." Suno and Udio are building their defenses around fair use. In the Massachusetts case against Suno, both sides plan to file for summary judgment on fair use.

SymphonyOS has released SymphonyOS V2, its biggest update since launch. The platform, which calls itself 'music's agent company,' has rebuilt its entire marketing toolset around six specialized AI agents. Each agent handles one part of an artist's career or one stage of a label's release process.

The SymphonyOS team has run artist campaigns since 2016. It built sites and marketing infrastructure for SZA, Travis Scott and 21 Savage, then released SymphonyOS V1 in 2022. Where V1 focused on smart links, evergreen presaves and automated ads, V2 turns the product itself into a multi-agent AI workforce that plans and executes work in place of a team.
Maestro coordinates the other agents. Artists and teams give instructions by text, email or chat. Simmy runs ads on TikTok, YouTube, Instagram, Facebook and Spotify.
Cue manages releases, building a rollout plan by working backward from the release date. Echo maps an artist's fan base to find superfans and handles the messages sent out to them.
Maude handles business affairs, including analyzing royalty statements and flagging discrepancies. Sage runs creator campaigns.

Music marketing teams have long used AI tools to speed up their work, but the limits were clear: without current strategy knowledge or real performance data, the advice stayed generic. SymphonyOS V2's agents were trained directly by the SymphonyOS team and draw on campaign data from a platform used by more than 100,000 people, from DIY artists to major-label acts, since launch.

Agentic AI has been more buzzword than substance for a while, with no example in music that plausibly worked. Music Ally calls SymphonyOS V2 the most promising case it has seen so far and is testing it with a few artists it works with.

Two things are worth watching: how much human oversight the agents need in sensitive areas like ad budgets and fan messaging, and how ownership and use of the data teams feed into the platform gets settled.

Similar tools exist. Fan engagement platform Laylo has released automated AI agents that each handle one marketing or sales task, such as a UGC agent, a ticket sales agent and a cart abandonment agent. More platforms are also opening MCP servers that connect their data to general-purpose AI assistants like Claude, Gemini and ChatGPT. Openstage MCP connects an artist's real-time fan data, streaming analytics and mailing list.

The difference is structural. SymphonyOS V2 is an all-in-one suite priced at roughly $49 to $99 a month that gives teams finished specialized agents up front, which teams then feed by connecting ad accounts, streaming platforms and fan lists. The MCP approach runs in reverse: teams pick an AI platform, build their own agents, then choose servers to connect. Teams with little experience in releases, advertising or creator campaigns may be better served by SymphonyOS, which comes with music knowledge already built in.

blocks.cap: Depth Field — the result of overlapping Ghost and Xray

blocks.x: Let's step away for a moment from the surveillance-tech nightmare around us. There's a kind of computer vision that runs locally, not online, and is built for creation and art. Resolume 7.28 adds Wire nodes powered by vision, along with new effects and blends. It removes backgrounds, segments people, and estimates depth — and it's clean and fun.
Underneath are two Wire building blocks. One is Human Segmentation, meaning image segmentation, and the other is Depth Estimation.

With just these two, 7.28 ships a ready-to-use set of higher-level effects and a new Depth Blend mode. Since it's all built in Wire, you can take it apart, learn from it, and modify it. You can even build your own effects.

Background removal, strictly speaking, is background separation using human segmentation. The resulting mask can be used for anything. Depth estimation pulls depth from a single 2D image, so no extra camera is needed. From this come Depth blur (fake depth of field), Depth field (overlapping Ghost and Xray), Depth displace (using depth as displacement), Depth pixelation, and Depth shift (cutting image layers based on the depth map).

Depth Blend Mode blends using the depth map instead of opacity. MIDI/OSC monitoring has also improved, and in Wire, as in Arena, a right-click now restores default values. Resolume says it's reworking its audio engine, and picked Arena's FFT audio reactivity as the first step. Wire is getting an audio spectrum feature and path drawing, and the next release, 7.29, will add a few new slice effects.

People used to go to all kinds of lengths to fake this effect. A few years ago, the writer did a dance piece in Jitter, pulling motion from a difference image and using it as a displacement map, tuning it so the dancer's movement looked like depth.

These examples show why using vision for creative work is fundamentally different from surveillance. In the end, what's being handled is human perception, and computer vision is just a channel that lets you work intuitively with pixel data. Above all, it runs locally. Interaction design, too, should be opt-in rather than opt-out — building a playground where people choose for themselves to stand in front of the camera.

Resolume recently added AI assistance in its 7.26 update. As expected, reactions were sharply divided, and the company admitted in this week's newsletter that it has been "received with complicated feelings in the Resolume community" and that "we know not everyone likes AI." It then immediately pivoted to touting productivity gains.

That response misses the point. People who reject AI aren't doubting whether productivity goes up. They're asking whether working fast is really the goal. Going through an effect patch node by node, tweaking values, and making mistakes is itself the work. The ability to handle things quickly and efficiently is something built up over a long time, without MCP.

There's also an objection that has nothing to do with speed. OpenAI and Anthropic are tied up in defense applications, including for the U.S. military, and environmental concerns persist. On top of that, unlike past technologies, AI tools can't be owned — you're locked into monthly subscriptions and credits. This isn't saying don't use MCP. It means the conversation needs to go further than just "it's faster."
Nagi is a new desktop app for designing and building native audio plugins. There's no need to write code directly.
The workflow combines a visual node editor, Faust DSP code, and an interface designer in one app. Audio preview is built in, so you can hear how a patch sounds before compiling.

The node editor provides audio, MIDI, and parameter ports. Features like oscillators, filters, dynamics, reverb, chorus, flanger, de-essing, formant filtering, and stereo imaging come as ready-made nodes. If you need finer control over the DSP, you can drop from the visual graph into Faust code.

There's also an AI assistant. Ask it in your normal way of speaking, and it writes Faust DSP code or a GUI layout. It runs locally, and the result can be added to an existing project or used to replace it entirely.
Knob, slider, and button nodes bind directly to parameters. The app fully supports the Faust standard library, and includes syntax highlighting and inline diagnostics.

The GUI designer includes knobs, sliders, buttons, meters, and spectrum displays. It also uses envelope displays, filmstrip animation, keyboards, and a preset browser. Each widget has its own range, skew, and response curve.

Builds output native VST3 and CLAP. It supports Windows, macOS, and Linux, and the macOS build ships as a universal binary covering both Intel and Apple Silicon. MIDI instrument plugins can be built too. Project files are stored locally, and no account is needed even to build.

Nagi is currently in public beta. The core app can be downloaded for free to patch and build plugins, and no account is needed for these features. During the beta, the Nagi Pro evaluation license is listed at $0 and covers up to three devices. Final pricing has not yet been announced.

Starting Wednesday, Spotify began rolling out a new 'Taste Profile' feature to US Premium subscribers, following a beta in New Zealand. Turning it on shows how Spotify understands your listening taste, and you can use natural-language requests to an AI to fine-tune your recommendations.

Taste Profile runs on Spotify's AI. It was first unveiled at SXSW, when only users in New Zealand could try it in beta. Now that it's coming to the US, it faces its biggest test yet in Spotify's largest market for traffic and revenue.

TechCrunch compared the feature to being handed the key to Spotify's algorithm. Taste Profile shows the criteria the platform uses to serve up music and audio, covering Discover Weekly and Made for You recommendations as well as the yearly talking point, Spotify Wrapped.

The problem is that those recommendations don't always keep pace with changing tastes. If users can edit their profile directly, Spotify can pinpoint more precisely what needs to change. Requests can boost or dial back specific genres or artists, or ask for more variety in the mix.
It also filters out things you listen to often but don't want recommended, such as sleep sounds or music played for kids in the car.

There was already a way to exclude specific content from recommendations, but it meant removing tracks or playlists one at a time. Now, by talking to Spotify's AI, you can specify the kind of content you want to see less of. Instead of pinpointing a track, you can simply describe the 'mood' you want.

In the mobile app, tapping your profile photo and scrolling down brings up Taste Profile. There, you can check how Spotify currently reads your taste. Writing conversationally under 'Tell us more' about what you'd like adjusted gets reflected "within a few hours."
The feature is still in beta. The US rollout is a good way to work out remaining bugs. Spotify hasn't said when it will expand to a wider range of regions.

blocks.cap: LANDR co-founder and CEO Pascal Pilon and CTO Tommy Desilets

blocks.x: LANDR said the volume of artificial streams Spotify flagged on music it distributes dropped 95% between Q1 2025 and Q2 2026.

That's according to a press release the Montreal-based distribution and music-production platform issued on Tuesday, September 22. In the same release, the company said it is expanding a streaming fraud detection system built with Quebec AI lab Mila.

Mila is a Montreal-based nonprofit AI research institute founded by Yoshua Bengio, who co-won the 2018 A.M. Turing Award for deep learning research. The early machine learning model was developed and deployed by Édouard Demotes-Mainard, and operation and development were later taken over by LANDR's fraud prevention team.

Still, the 95% drop isn't the achievement of the Mila system alone. LANDR describes it as the result of running several fraud-prevention measures together. One model scores accounts using profile and behavioral data, while another looks for patterns in listening activity that wouldn't occur with a genuine audience.

This expansion's focus is on catching things earlier. Accounts with unusually high release frequency, catalogs that appear overnight, clusters of accounts sharing devices or payout information, and metadata crafted to impersonate known artists are now flagged further upstream.

"Finding fraud by hand at our scale was like looking for a needle in a haystack. Our first-generation models turned that into something manageable," said LANDR CTO Tommy Desilets. "Now we're moving that capability earlier in the distribution process, so the team gets better signals before a suspicious release ever reaches a streaming service."

LANDR defines fake streams as plays generated without any genuine listening intent, typically driven by bots, stream farms, or hijacked accounts. Since April 2024, Spotify has charged labels and distributors a per-track fee when content is caught engaging in "blatant artificial streaming."
"Artificial streams aren't just gaming a platform. They compete for the same royalty pool that should go to musicians trying to make a living," said co-founder and CEO Pascal Pilon.

Flagged activity is reviewed by the fraud-prevention team before any action is taken, since an unusual pattern in the data isn't by itself proof of fraud. Pilon said, "We want AI to help our team make better judgment calls at scale, not replace people. Sometimes a song really is just blowing up — the artist is having a really good day."

Machine learning is only one layer of this system. ACRCloud fingerprints recordings against commercial catalogs, and Ircam Amplify's technology, which released an AI-generated music detector in 2024, examines recordings for signs of tampering and acoustic traces of synthetic generation.

Identity verification is also being introduced for accounts with frequent releases. Artists disclose at registration whether a release was AI-generated, and that information travels to streaming services in the metadata — a disclosure pathway Spotify began rolling out with DDEX in September 2025.

LANDR says this expansion is aligned with IFPI's Streaming Integrity Initiative, announced September 14. "The goal is simple," Pilon said. "Stop fraud earlier without adding friction for legitimate artists."

Startup brand Melofty has released the Axom Max audio processor. It packs new modeling technology, a 'real-time' tracking guitar synth, an AI assistant that builds rigs, and possible NAM-A2 support. Gearnews says it does everything short of selling merch at the venue.
It's notable that 'Guitar' was dropped from the product name. That signals it's aimed at a wider range of musicians, not just guitarists.

Each amp and pedal capture made with Melofty's proprietary MFIM (Multidimensional Fusion Inverse Modeling) technology contains up to 9,856 parameter points. Players who want to dive straight in can choose from more than 400 amps, more than 130 effects, and more than 200 IRs.

blocks.cap: The AI assistant used via smartphone app

blocks.x: If there's too much to choose from, the smartphone AI assistant can handle it. Type or speak a request like '80s British Stadium Rock' or '70s Psychedelic,' and it produces a signal chain linking virtual pedals, amps, and IRs, matched as closely as possible to the desired tone.

There's also DeepSynth, a synth for guitar and bass. It tracks pitch in real time without a MIDI pickup, and includes over 50 synth sounds plus instrument modeling that makes a guitar sound like other instruments (a feature similar to the Boss VG-800).

Up to 19 effects can be applied to a single preset. By routing two inputs separately, guitar and bass can also be played at the same time on one unit. There are 504 preset slots, with up to 6 scenes per preset.

It also includes a stereo looper that records up to 60 minutes, plus vocal effects like tuning, harmonizer, and reverb. Control centers on a 7-inch touchscreen, with 8 footswitches, 4 knobs, and an expression pedal. Connected to a computer, it becomes an 8-in/8-out audio interface.

It is priced at 1,299 euros. Thomann is taking orders, with shipping expected in 2-3 weeks. Right out of the gate it's priced to compete with Tonex, Helix Stadium, and Quad Cortex, which Gearnews called a bold move, adding that it is waiting for the first reviews.

blocks.cap: Spotify and Meta's AI agent Muse

blocks.x: Spotify has detailed how it works inside Meta's personal AI agent Muse. Linking the two services lets users talk with Muse to play music, save songs, and build Spotify playlists.

Spotify has been one of Muse's connectors since the agent launched on September 8. At the time, Meta's chief AI officer Alexandr Wang listed it alongside Gmail, Google Calendar, OpenTable and Plaid. Spotify posted the integration details on its blog on September 23, the same day Meta put Muse at the center of its product strategy in the Menlo Park Connect keynote.

Spotify describes it this way: "The agent can play music on Spotify, save songs to your library, build playlists, and help find books or podcasts. It's all done through conversation." The example given is a road trip: you can ask it to build a driving playlist suited to your destination and have it start playing the moment you leave. It can also resume a podcast you left off, or play a saved playlist through your kitchen speaker.
Muse can also create a 'Personal Podcast' that turns daily briefings, notes or ideas into audio and adds them to your Spotify library.

Muse runs on a dedicated virtual machine Meta calls the Muse Secure VM, powered by a model called Muse Spark. It first launched in the US on iOS, Android and muse.ai, followed by a Mac version on September 17 and a Canada launch the next day. The Spotify integration is also limited to the US and Canada for now. Meta says it checks with users first before sensitive actions like sending emails or making payments.

For Spotify, this extends a strategy of using other tech companies' AI assistants as distribution channels. The company said "Spotify is already available on more than 2,000 devices, from cars, TVs and speakers to ChatGPT and Claude." It added recommendation features to ChatGPT in October 2025, and struck a similar deal with Anthropic's Claude this past April.
Meanwhile, Amazon has blocked Muse from shopping on its site, citing data security and disclosure concerns. Spotify described the integration as "just the beginning."

blocks.cap: San Jose Sharks pull a goal song accused of being AI-generated

blocks.x: The NHL's San Jose Sharks are changing their goal song. The new track arrives on October 1. The previous goal song, 'Power Bite,' lasted exactly one season. Allegations that it was AI-made sparked a strong backlash from fans.

The backlash grew louder after online sleuths pointed out the song was likely made with Suno, the AI music platform that is as controversial as it is popular. The Sharks ultimately decided to drop the song.

Hockey teams typically have a dedicated song that plays when a goal is scored at their home arena. Since their inaugural season in 1993, the Sharks had used Gary Glitter's arena-rock staple 'Rock and Roll, Part 2.'

'Power Bite' was reportedly chosen by fans, but it drew criticism for sounding 'cheap.' Critics also accused the team of picking a bland, 'soulless' track to save on licensing fees for well-known arena hits.

The term 'AI slop' gained traction after online sleuths found that BVRNOUT appeared to have made the track with Suno. Fan frustration grew further when the team did not directly address the allegations.
And now the Sharks have ended the 'Power Bite' era. In a new video, defenseman Sam Dickonson switches off the speaker that played the song and announces, "The new goal song arrives on October 1."
Digital Music News predicted that the Sharks will not make their next goal song with AI.

Sony Music Group has joined ARIAM (Alliance for Responsible Innovation in the Arts & Media), an AI policy coalition. It is the first music company to do so. ARIAM launched in June 2026 with member companies from film, TV, journalism, publishing, education and technology.

The move was announced on September 23 by ARIAM president Victoria Furniss. Existing members include The Walt Disney Company, Fox Entertainment, ITV, BBC, Adobe, Condé Nast, Financial Times and The New York Times.

Sony Music Entertainment COO Kevin Kelleher said, "Generative AI is both a major opportunity and a challenge for artists and songwriters," adding, "We joined ARIAM to help shape how AI fits into the future across the creative industries." He added that Sony fully shares ARIAM's view that the only foundation is a healthy licensing environment in which responsible AI companies partner with rights holders first.
Furniss welcomed the move, saying, "The issues surrounding AI span the entire creative community, and music is an essential part of that conversation."

ARIAM says it aims to work with the content and technology industries to build legal and policy frameworks that are 'responsible by design,' going beyond copyright to protect consumers, especially children, and creators. It is headquartered in Los Angeles and led by Furniss, a former Netflix and Warner Bros. executive.
Music Ally quipped that ARIAM's self-description—"an outcomes-focused, solutions-oriented global coalition spanning the content industries"—must have gone through quite a few rounds of sign-off.

Sony Music Entertainment is the only major label that has not signed licensing deals with Suno or Udio. It filed a second lawsuit against Udio on July 20, and on September 18 sued Suno again alongside Universal Music Group.
Fred again.. said he is opposed to using AI in music.

The British DJ and producer posted several Instagram Stories on September 25. The post revisited thoughts on AI that he had written in his phone's notes app a year earlier. "I've been thinking about this for a while, and the opposite of AI music might not be human music. It's making music."

"The process is the magic. Anyone lucky enough to have made music, or anything, has probably felt this in their own way for a long time. That's probably why I've never felt any urge to try AI. I put a lot of my identity into the process, and I've never felt that was a bad choice."
He also said the process of coming up with ideas and making music is a kind of 'meditation' for him. "Handing that process to a machine fundamentally conflicts with what I love about this work."

The post ended like this: "Clumsily but persistently rolling toward one idea. Trying endlessly, for hours, for years, to make something you wish existed. That's the greatest luck we get to have. There's a lot I worry AI might threaten, but never this."
Skrillex and Daft Punk's Thomas Bangalter have also recently voiced reservations about AI publicly.
Earlier this month, Fred again.. was named as a contributing artist on the GTA VI soundtrack, with the track 'Sexy Magic' featuring PinkPantheress, Etienne de Crécy, and CA7RIEL & Paco Amoroso.

Music startup Thoughtful Things has launched a Kickstarter campaign for its first instrument, Engram. It's a sampler and groovebox that uses AI to mangle incoming sound, and even hallucinate sounds that were never there.

But it's not a boxed-up Suno. It's nothing like a device that spits out radio top-40 songs at the push of a button. It's built to make experimental, strange sounds and push AI audio models past their limits.

Engram doesn't connect to the internet. Instead, it runs a “small AI” inside the device itself. According to the Kickstarter page, the model was designed and trained in-house. Here's how the company explains it.
“We trained our audio models on open datasets containing only audio cleared for commercial use, such as CC-BY. We have never trained on non-commercial, pirated, or stolen data, and we never will.”

The firmware will also be open, letting anyone tinker with it or upload their own models. In the campaign video, founder Evan King asks for “piano” by voice, and Engram spits out a glitchy, hazy approximation of a piano.

King asks people to think of Engram as a “field recorder for latent space,” a machine for exploring AI hallucination and experimental sound design. Inspired by circuit bending, it can twist a small AI model until it breaks.

Thoughtful Things is offering only a limited number of Engram units on Kickstarter, starting at $675. The company hasn't disclosed the retail price, but the $675 backer price is listed as a 30% discount, suggesting it will likely land around $850 to $900.
ElevenLabs has released Studio 4.0, an agentic video editor built into ElevenCreative. It creates video, images, voice, music, and sound effects directly inside the project.

Describe the shot you need in text, and that shot lands on the timeline, placed alongside voiceover, music, and images. If you don't like it, you don't have to start over; you can just refine that one shot, and editing, captions, and export all happen in one place.

The timeline supports frame-level zoom and clip snapping, and moving clips doesn't throw off the sync. Captions are treated like any other clip: you can split a cue, merge two of them, or fix a mistranscribed word right away.
The AI co-editor, Studio Agent, drafts a cut from a single prompt. Users can take over editing at any point and hand it back to the agent again.

That doesn't mean AI is useless for audio work. Russ Hughes, founder of Production Expert, admits AI plays a big role in rescuing unusable audio and sorting hundreds of thousands of sound effects. Generative AI that fills in dropped sections during recording is useful too.

What he takes issue with is generative AI that produces music, writing, or images from a single prompt. The deeper he dug, he writes, the more he found that the technology is 'boring by design.' Models run on probability, guessing only the most likely answer a human might write, sing, or play.

Gated reverb is a good example. It came about when someone left the talkback mic on an SSL console switched on while working out a drum part. The location was the Stone Room at Townhouse Studios, and the talkback had a gate on it. Nobody was looking for that sound, but someone said 'that's not bad' and kept it, and it ended up on the record.

Generative AI is good at ruining things with hallucinations, but it can't create moments like this. When Hughes asked Suno for "music no one has ever heard," it produced three unremarkable pop songs. Asking for "something original" got the same result.

He draws a line against the argument that better algorithms will fix this. The structure itself, built to guess what comes next, is what produces predictable answers. Loosening the temperature value only produces garbage instead of magical accidents.

To the question of whether humans are also influenced by what they've seen and heard, he calls that a 'false equivalence.' Human creation comes from experience; generative AI comes from pattern. Suno can sing about loss but has never felt loss.
As a final experiment, Hughes played his wife the Suno output. She said she didn't like it, then, without being asked, asked back, "Is this AI?"

Last month's deal between Suno and BMG became a test that splits how artists really feel about AI. Mötley Crüe is on the okay side. Manager Allen Kovac said the band would “opt in if it's a paid deal,” adding that “AI promotes music, it doesn't dilute it.”

Not everyone is this optimistic. Suno touts a $5.4 billion valuation, 2 million paying users, and 100 million users who have made a song. The BMG deal includes an opt-in clause that artists choose themselves, but music attorney Dina LaPolt said “none of our clients would do that.” She praised BMG for choosing opt-in over opt-out.

Besides BMG, WMG and Believe have also partnered with Suno, which unveiled its v6 model on September 9. On September 18, UMG and Sony Music filed a new lawsuit adding 61,000 songs, calling v6 “fruit from the same poisoned tree.”

How each deal actually secures artist consent remains unclear. Attorney Harold Pappineau pointed out that, depending on contract terms, some artists may not be able to opt out. BMG's Celine Joshua drew a line, saying “this is not a blanket deal without consent.”

Attorney Ben McLane, who represents Afroman and others, called it “the way of the future” and said he would advise clients to take part. The real question is royalty splits, and none of the deal announcements spell out what songwriters and artists get.

Eric Greenspan, who represents Red Hot Chili Peppers, Dead & Company, and the E Street Band, advises always building an opt-out right into any deal. “Suno and Udio both keep rolling out new plans. It's the wild, wild West while artists, labels, and tech companies hunt for a business model.”

Composer Michael Whalen believes we've been asking the wrong questions about generative AI. More important than whether AI will replace musicians or whether Suno survives its lawsuits is the fact that the music industry is splitting in two.

One side is synthetic music, made fast, consumed fast, and swapped out just as quickly. The other is artist music, where identity, ownership, history, and fan relationships still matter most. Blue Dot Music founder Nicholas Gunn agrees. "We're entering an era where two kinds of music business coexist."

AI solved a scarcity problem the music industry never actually had. Music has always been abundant. What was scarce was attention, trust, cultural presence, and the relationship between artists and audiences. AI increased supply but failed to increase demand.

Synthetic music can still be a big business, in places with a clear use: playlists, games, fitness, meditation, in-store background audio. But that isn't an artist career. On the artist side, direct relationships with fans—websites, mailing lists, live shows, physical merchandise—matter more than ever.

Both worlds will likely remain on streaming platforms, increasingly distinguished by AI labeling. Whalen believes metadata will mark the difference before the day comes when no one can tell the difference at all.

The Suno lawsuits are where 'music AI 1.0' and '2.0' collide. Warner and BMG have signed licensing deals, and Suno itself said it would retire older models once next-generation ones arrive. The market is demanding licensing before any court has even ruled.

That could leave songs made with early models as 'stranded tracks.' They wouldn't become illegal, but once distributors, music supervisors, and catalog buyers start asking about provenance, moving them elsewhere gets harder. Whalen's conclusion is short: music that can travel is worth more than music that can't.

blocks.cap: Musixmatch founder and CEO Massimo 'Max' Ciociola

blocks.x: Call Musixmatch just a 'lyrics company' and Massimo 'Max' Ciociola might tilt his head. It's true the company built its name organizing lyrics in songs. Now it works with nearly 250,000 rights holders and is used by more than 80 million people worldwide. The lyrics scrolling beneath songs on Spotify, YouTube, Apple Music and Instagram belong to this company.

Collecting and monitoring lyrics in more than 250 languages has already turned it into a 'sophisticated royalty management company,' he says. 'We've evolved into a kind of fintech company. Our core business is processing royalties.' The next goal is a company that manages rights through multiple AI agents to protect rights holders and songwriters.

In October 2025, Musixmatch signed 'AI innovation' agreements with the three major publishers, securing a catalog of 15 million songs. This March, it launched Sentinel, a real-time copyright-detection service for UGC platforms. It flags even partial lyric infringement as a user types a prompt, with a verdict in under 100 milliseconds.

Its first major client is Suno. Suno confirmed in August that it had adopted Sentinel. When a Suno user tries to make music by entering lyrics from an existing song, Sentinel filters it out. Musixmatch has positioned itself as neutral infrastructure, selling to rights holders who want to protect their catalogs and AI companies that want to stay within the law. It also unveiled Music Lens, an AI 'music agent' that lets publishers analyze the meaning, mood and context of their catalogs.

The NMPA estimated that in 2024, lyrics licensing accounted for only 1% of publisher and songwriter income. Ciociola believes that figure badly undersells the potential of lyrics. 'In the language of AI, lyrics are becoming the LLM of the music industry. They're literally the language of music.' He says that within a few years, searches by song title will shift to prompts like 'make me a playlist of breakup songs,' with lyrics at the center of it.

On the rights holders' lawsuits against Anthropic and Suno, he said he is 'entirely on the side of IP owners.' He predicted Anthropic will settle with music rights holders, adding, 'It has to be fixed, and it will be.'

VirtualDJ 2026 has received its third and final update. AI features have grown again. Alongside Shoutouts, which lets users create their own voiceovers and lyrics, a feature that writes scripts from simple text descriptions has been added.

VirtualDJ 2026 was built from its first version with AI integration at its center. A Gearnews writer argues the new features add little to traditional mixing. But if you see mixing as the complete 'atomization' of music, it opens up entirely new, perhaps slightly unsettling possibilities. Atomix says it isn't chasing trends but adding AI features that are genuinely useful to DJs.

In the second update, which followed the December launch, AI automatically generated visuals that moved in sync with the beat. A fluid beatgrid and BPM stabilization feature also arrived then, along with improved AI lyric recognition.
The new Shoutouts feature lets users insert their own voiceovers and lyrics into a track as it plays. Custom drops, live edits and announcements are all handled without leaving the DJ software.

AI Scripting lets DJs build their own customizations and extensions inside the software without programming skills. Writing a prompt in plain language produces a script, letting users reshape controls and workflows their own way. Much as Ableton Live released extensions, other apps are likely to follow a similar path.
Compatibility with various DJ controllers has improved, and support for some streaming services, including Spotify, has expanded. VirtualDJ 2026 users again receive the update for free.
Today brought an unusual cluster of interesting, creative uses of AI in music. After Engram, ClassicalBot is the next story in the news. It's a project started by Slovak developer Robert Druska.

He first built it to map classical concerts in his home country, then expanded it worldwide. He wrote on the site: "From the start, this project was an experiment in how far AI automation could go. Almost everything you see here — source discovery, extracting concert information, program analysis — is handled by AI in some way."

How it works is detailed in a blog post, which introduces concepts like a 'magic box' and a 'crawler factory.' Druska believes the technology he built can be used outside music too. "The idea of an automated crawler factory can be extended to any purpose. You could build a loop to scrape every restaurant menu in a city, online shop prices, job listings, every kind of event, or corporate data."

ClassicalBot, first introduced by the Bliss music library management blog, shows how much a single developer can build. Whether it turns into a business remains to be seen. Still, it's an interesting case that might push others to build something of their own.

Oliver Thor is shaking up sound. Together with the duo MIRA新伝統, he bends the tempo of Ableton Live and builds drum kits out of YouTube chaos trawled by AI. The founder of the Glazmo Network, Thor has spent years digging into the “mythology of sound,” and he has just released two tools that anyone who enjoys uncertainty and glitches should grab.
CDM first came to know Thor through Bastl Instruments. He went on to work as a producer and now lives in Athens, where he shares his sound design process on the Glazmo Network Discord.

Agitator, made by MIRA新伝統 and Thor, grabs hold of a project's entire tempo and shakes it. Feed it audio and it resets the whole project tempo, with slew controls for smoothing, rise, and fall. Just set a minimum and maximum value and drop it on a track. It works like Ableton's Envelope Follower, except the stock device can't touch tempo. It costs €3 (pay more if you like) and requires Ableton Live 12 or later plus Max for Live.
GLAZMO_DREAM_PORT twists the black box of AI prompting. Generated Zen koan fragments become YouTube search terms, and the returned audio gets chopped up and loaded onto pads.

Hit the encryption button and it can flip into a glitchier, dreamier “corrupted” version. The plugin also generates provenance information so you can clear rights before release. It exchanges files with its host via drag and drop, and it's macOS-only, supporting VST3 for both Apple Silicon and Intel.

Michael Smith, a North Carolina man who admitted to using bots to play AI-generated songs billions of times and collect more than $8 million in royalties, has asked a federal judge to spare him prison time. According to Billboard, his lawyers want a sentence of probation.

His lawyers filed a sentencing memo at Manhattan federal court on September 22. They argue Smith's conduct caused only “a vanishingly small, unmeasurable loss” spread across millions of songwriters and artists. “The impact of one play of one artist's song on the market share of every other artist is a drop in the ocean, not a drop in a bucket. No artist or songwriter suffered any discernible harm from Mr. Smith's conduct.” The memo also claims 'major labels' did the same thing.

They asked the judge to weigh his lack of a criminal record, his history of good conduct, and the impact imprisonment would have on his family. “He made a serious mistake here, but that mistake does not define who he is.”

Smith pleaded guilty in March to one count of conspiracy to commit wire fraud. The maximum sentence is five years in prison. Federal sentencing guidelines call for 46 to 57 months, while the U.S. Probation Office's pre-sentence report recommended a shorter 24 months. Prosecutors have not yet filed a sentencing position. Under his plea agreement, Smith also agreed to forfeit more than $8 million. His sentencing, originally set for July 29, did not take place, and no new date appears in the public record.

Whatever sentence Judge John G. Koeltl hands down will be the first in the U.S. for AI-enabled streaming fraud. This type of criminal prosecution was also a first for the country. U.S. Attorney Jay Clayton has said, “the songs and the listeners were fake, but the millions of dollars Smith stole were real.”

Smith was first indicted in September 2024 on three counts: wire fraud, conspiracy to commit wire fraud, and conspiracy to commit money laundering. Prosecutors say he made the songs together with the unnamed CEO of an AI music company and a music promoter. According to the indictment, Smith calculated that bots could generate about 661,440 streams a day and $1,207,128 in annual royalties.

ABYZOR has added a free local AI module to Genesis, its MIDI-generation plugin for macOS and Windows. Genesis, released in June, is a plugin that creates melodies, basslines, chord progressions and arpeggios. You edit the results, then drag them into your DAW.
The new module does not replace the existing generator. It runs as an optional engine alongside Genesis v2.2.0, so the original procedural MIDI generation still works without the module.

Installing the module turns a single Genesis pattern into several versions. Transform mode keeps the original mood, Pitch Remix changes the notes while keeping the rhythm, and Keep Groove draws new material from the existing groove. You can run a whole pattern or pick specific bars, which is useful for growing ideas. The output is editable MIDI, so you can fix awkward notes and keep only the parts you like.

The engine runs locally on CPU or GPU and works offline once installed. There are no generation credits, API keys or subscription fees. ABYZOR said it plans to keep the module free going forward. The current beta uses the MIDI-GPT conversion pipeline, a symbolic music model aimed at bar-level infilling and controlled MIDI generation rather than finished audio.

If you don't have Genesis yet, you need to download two things. The email field on the Genesis download form is optional and can be left blank. The separate AI module installer is about 93MB for Windows and about 43MB for macOS. The installer then downloads the local engine from Hugging Face. According to ABYZOR's documentation, the engine package is roughly 400MB to 3GB, so the total size is far larger than the first installer file.

ABYZOR warns that this is still a public beta, so behavior and compatibility may change. Windows support covers 64-bit Windows 10 and 11. The macOS AI module is currently Apple Silicon only and unsigned, so you may need to click "Open Anyway" in Privacy & Security to launch it. Genesis ships as VST3 on Windows and VST3/AU on macOS. The AI module is not a plugin format; it's a separate local engine that runs on its own.
Suno posted a short clip showing Suno Studio. The caption is two lines: it says that recording your voice in Suno Studio can turn it into "anything," and that an electric guitar is "just the start."
In the video, the creator says he wants to add a short electric guitar moment between parts of the song, and suggests singing it in first. The hummed melody comes back as guitar sound.
A well-known Japanese actor and anime voice actor has filed a lawsuit against TikTok. The trigger was a series of videos suspected of using an AI-cloned version of his voice.

In Japan's anime industry, voice actors are sometimes loved as much as the characters they play. Kenjiro Tsuda, known for Jujutsu Kaisen and Yu-Gi-Oh!, is one such case. He may be the first Japanese voice actor to take a major company to court over alleged AI voice cloning. The video series in question carries narration that bears a striking resemblance to his voice; he is 55 this year.

According to court records, TikTok counters that the voice is just an "ordinary male voice," saying any resemblance to Tsuda's distinctive "glossy" baritone is subjective. But the anonymous account in question posted photos resembling a Jujutsu Kaisen character Tsuda voices.

The videos pair images with narration about urban legends and conspiracy theories; the narration is believed to be AI-generated. Tsuda's legal team estimates the account once had more than 200,000 subscribers and likely earned more than 500,000 yen (about $3,200) a month. The team argues the account "gained popularity only by reading suspicious, low-quality content in the appealing voice of a popular character."

Yuko Sasaki, managing director of the Japan Federation of Actors, said an actor's voice is "the result of years of harsh training and practice" and is "refined with a great deal of time and money." She added that courts "should recognize ownership of one's voice as a basic right," and that the union "fully supports" Tsuda.

TikTok challenges Tsuda's "nationwide fame" and recognition from the outset. It also denies that the account violated Japan's Unfair Competition Prevention Act by riding on an already-known brand. The company's position is that it merely provides "a space within the bounds of freedom of expression where users post creative and quirky content," seeking to play down its role in any infringement.

Tatsuhiro Ueno, a professor researching intellectual property at Waseda University, said the chance Tsuda would fail to be recognized as having a publicity right over his voice is "very low." He said his voice is "well known even in Europe" thanks to the ongoing popularity of Jujutsu Kaisen, and predicted the case would draw international attention as well.

blocks.x: “It's rainy today, make me a soft ballad that fits the season.” One line of prompt is enough to produce a convincing song in seconds. That is the power of Suno, the generative AI music service with over 100 million subscribers. Foreign outlets such as The New York Times (NYT), Financial Times (FT), and The Wall Street Journal (WSJ) have each covered the ripple effects AI has had on the music industry and the shaken notion of 'authenticity'.

According to the FT, French streaming platform Deezer said more than half of the tracks newly uploaded last July, an average of 90,000 songs a month, were AI-generated. A bigger problem is 'streaming fraud,' in which tracks are mass-produced with AI and play counts are inflated with bots. Deezer said last year up to 85% of streams of 100% AI-generated tracks were fraudulent.

Major labels such as Sony, Universal, and Warner have sued Suno, alleging it trained on millions of copyrighted works without permission. Yet Warner Music and others are reportedly already investing in AI model development through licensing deals with Suno and Udio. The NYT described AI as, for the existing industry, “both a 'pirate' to be sued and a 'partner' to team up with for new revenue.”

blocks.x: The WSJ noted that K-pop agencies are betting heavily on virtual artists and AI vocal technology. Virtual IP, free of privacy scandals or fatigue, is the perfect 'risk hedge' for capital. But the WSJ warned of eroded authenticity, saying “artists and fans are grappling with what they stand to lose because of it.” One fan called the AI technology that can perfectly polish even the worst singer a 'disaster' and drew a line against supporting it. The more AI music floods in, the more fans crave the imperfect, real sweat of someone breathing the same air.

Korea has a large institutional gap. Copyright bodies such as BMI in the US and GEMA in Europe have set distribution standards that split out human creative contribution. The Korea Music Copyright Association tried to allow trust registration for human-led AI music, but regulators stepped in and it was withdrawn just 22 days after taking effect. Meanwhile, 'AI slop' music made to dodge background-music royalties at cafes and restaurants is seeping into daily life.

The column calls for creator-protection systems to be quickly aligned with global standards. It warns that the moment the premium of a human artist's story and on-stage presence is lost, fans' wallets close too.
ElevenLabs released two new voice models on Monday, ElevenLabs v4 and v4 Turbo. They offer finer control over expression, cut latency for voice agents, and support more than 90 languages.

The company unveiled v3 last year and previewed this new model earlier this year at an event in Warsaw. The v4 generation uses a new architecture, giving tighter control and faster cloning. According to the company, just 10 seconds of audio is enough to clone a voice.

On the creative side, it holds onto a voice's identity better even across long text. It reads text aloud while adjusting expression based on the context of the writing. The company also expanded the inline expression tags introduced in v3; stacking multiple tags now lets the model follow their order.
Supported languages grew from 70 in the previous version to 90. The languages with the biggest quality gains were Japanese, Brazilian Portuguese, Mandarin and Cantonese.

ElevenLabs has rapidly grown its enterprise calling business over the past year. More than 55% of revenue now comes from large companies. The company says the new models have low enough latency for smooth conversation, making them well suited to voice agents. As soon as the LLM running behind the scenes starts generating an answer, audio generation begins, and situations like complaints, escalation to a supervisor, or being put on hold are handled differently, solving problems more effectively.

Competition among voice models has heated up. Startups like Cartesia, Deepgram, Fish Audio, Bosun and WellSaid Labs have released expressive voice models, and Google and OpenAI have also upgraded their voice models.

ElevenLabs raised $500 million from Sequoia earlier this year at a $11 billion valuation. Rumors are also circulating about a follow-on round at a $22 billion valuation. Annualized revenue jumped from about $330 million at the start of the year to more than $600 million. Aggressive hiring in India, Europe and Brazil has pushed headcount past 800. Co-founder and CEO Mati Staniszewski said in a recent TechCrunch interview that the company plans to go public "within the next few years," though he did not give a specific timeline.

blocks.x: On June 22, 2026, a global coalition of artists, songwriters, and managers issued an open letter opposing how labels and publishers license AI music. The core point: "Labels and publishers insist AI companies must get permission to train on their catalogs, while denying artists and songwriters that same right."

The letter raises three problems: artists are told they are automatically enrolled in AI use with little real choice, new-artist contracts default to 'unlimited, exclusive rights' clauses for AI training, and training (input) is distinguished from output while training requirements are barely mentioned.

The coalition, which includes Music Artists Coalition, Songwriters of North America, and The Ivors Academy, demands three principles: specific consent and control, fair compensation and transparent distribution, and clear requests with defined purpose, duration, and the right to withdraw. The letter closes by saying "the future of music must be built with artists, songwriters, and their representatives, not imposed on them."
IFPI countered that music companies protect artists' interests by suing over unauthorized AI use and running licensing models that return revenue to creators.

A search tool built by The Atlantic now lets you check whether a musician's work was used to train AI models. The database is based on reporting by Atlantic journalist Alex Reisner. He recently identified four major music datasets used in AI development and made them searchable to anyone.

Together, the four datasets hold millions of songs, from famous artists to independent musicians to underground producers. Two are especially large, holding about 12 million and 9 million songs respectively, and the other two each have more than 100,000 songs.

According to Reisner, the datasets have already been downloaded "thousands of times." Google and Stability AI have acknowledged using some of the material in research papers. Some sources, like the Free Music Archive dataset, allow personal listening but require a license for commercial use.

Reisner sees the datasets as ultimately exposing a gap between how AI companies describe their data and how it's actually collected. Developers say they only used "freely available" material, but the reality is more complicated. Much of it circulates as "lists of track links" posted on YouTube or Spotify, and AI developers use automated tools to bulk-download the audio. Some of this bypasses mechanisms like logins or ads that generate revenue for creators. Reisner points out that "such tools violate these platforms' terms of service."

The result is a training landscape where commercially released music is technically abundant and accessible, but consent, compensation, and transparency remain murky. The argument that training on copyrighted material counts as "fair use" is also a line AI companies like Suno and Anthropic often invoke.

The datasets include music across genres and eras. Daft Punk, Aphex Twin, and Radiohead are in there, along with Wu-Tang Clan and Jack Antonoff. Antonoff has long opposed AI music production. "The idea of optimizing what we do completely misses the point," he said, adding that he and his colleagues "have never wanted this work to be faster or easier." Users can search The Atlantic's AI Watchdog tool for music, books, and other media that may have been used in AI training.
Apple unveiled the Music Understanding framework at WWDC 2026. It's a tool for analyzing audio on-device across Apple platforms.

The framework lets apps process audio and extract six musical elements along with timing information. AnalyzedRhythm captures beat positions, bar boundaries, and BPM tempo. Key finds the tonality (tonic and mode) of a given section. Loudness measures integrated, short-term, momentary, and peak loudness according to industry standards.

Pace measures perceived energy and drive using events per minute, separate from fixed tempo. Structure divides a track into structural sections, segments, and phrases. Instrument Activity identifies which instruments play and when.
A commenter named Palomorado raised concerns about education. "I can already picture ear-training class newcomers complaining, 'there's an app for this.'"
Two Notes Audio Engineering released Genome Intro, a free entry-level version, alongside Genome 2.0. It supports AU, VST3, and AAX formats for macOS and Windows.

It's packed with content despite being free: 4 amp models, 14 pedals, 5 cabinets, and 4 studio effects. The core is the CODEX AI amp playback engine, which loads and plays Neural Amp Modeller, AIDA-X, and Proteus captures on one screen.

The four stock amps are Albion '59 (Marshall Super Lead 1959), Gemini '64 (Fender Twin Reverb), Peggy '76 (Ampeg SVT 1796), and PVH50 (Peavey 5150). Among the pedals, classics like Green Mini (Ibanez TS9 Tube Screamer) and Foxy Wah 46 (Vox V846) stand out. The DynIR virtual cabinets include the Fender Bassman, Peavey 5150, and Ampeg V-9 bass cabinet, among others.

The studio effects consist of Studio Twin Tracker, EQ, reverb, and CODEX, plus a MIXFIT section for shaping tone. Pricing: Genome Intro is free, Genome is 129.99 euros (discounted to 89.99 euros), and Genome Suite is 299.99 euros (discounted to 159.99 euros).

The way music gets made is changing, as 'vibe coding' spreads, where you describe something to AI in words and it builds an audio plugin on the spot. Rick Rubin called this approach "the punk rock of software."

ChatDSP, built by Dylan Baston, is a Max for Live device for Ableton Live. It builds instruments, effects, and MIDI effects from text prompts and exposes up to 48 mappable parameters. Using the AI requires an API key and credits, and it now accepts local AI models in addition to Claude and ChatGPT.

Amorph, from Artists in DSP, is a free browser-based generator. It builds VST3 and AU plugins for Mac and PC that work with most major DAWs. It's currently in v0.99 beta, supporting custom UI generation and sample-accurate MIDI timing. The next version is expected to add direct AI communication and a marketplace feature.

Pluginmaker.ai also builds VST and AU plugins in the browser. You can test them in real time with MIDI, a keyboard, or a sequencer, and it runs on a credit-based subscription. There's also a marketplace (10% fee) for buying and selling plugins you've made, and it stands out for its polished graphical interface.

Leo Viascar-Caroni, CEO of Artists in DSP, said "writing code by hand will disappear within a few years," adding that "what's left is the fun part." Pluginmaker.ai co-founder Dominik Bilski said "the goal is to let anyone build the plugin they imagine at low cost." Dylan Baston, who made ChatDSP, added that "some of the criticism reminds me of classical musicians who hated keyboards, drum machines, and DAWs."

It isn't all rosy. The article also notes concerns: the environmental burden of data centers using up to 5 million gallons of water a day, training on copyrighted material without consent, threats to existing plugin developers' livelihoods, and worries that so-called 'AI slop' could lower production quality.

Hypebot covered the first AI Music Summit (AIMS) held by Berklee College of Music in a June 29 piece by Ryan Blakeley. Hundreds of industry figures gathered at the event, held in Boston from June 3 to 5, while outside, students protested the school's AI policy.

First, AI music is far broader than text-to-song generators. It spans assistive, generative and agentic applications across production, composition, stem separation, sampling, effects processing and royalty calculation. Elizabeth Moody pointed to a branding problem that comes from lumping different technologies together under one name.

Second, generative AI is both an evolution and a revolution. The phonograph, MIDI and streaming all shook up the industry too, but generative AI is unprecedented in democratizing music creation. 75,000 AI-generated tracks are uploaded to Deezer every day. That raises genuinely new challenges around copyright, NIL protections, and the pace at which technology is outrunning the law.

Third, it's fine to feel ambivalent. The discussion was balanced rather than uncritical advocacy. Composer Lucas Cantor Santiago criticized companies like Suno, saying it's "like solving a math problem no one asked," while strategist Drew Thurlow defended the creative possibilities of generative AI.

Fourth, artists need to be at the center. Holly Herndon, Jordan Rudess and L'Rain took part in performances and presentations. While AI companies raise enormous sums — Suno raised $400 million (a $5.4 billion valuation), ElevenLabs raised $500 million ($11 billion) — artists worry that sync placements and background-music work could disappear.

Fifth, a generational divide showed itself. Ahead of the summit, students opened the Instagram account @berkleeagainstai, which passed 1,000 followers within days. Theo Wheeler, who took part in the protest, said, "I want to know how to navigate this once I graduate and go to work. Where do our jobs go?"
Deezer unveiled a new feature that lets listeners remix songs within the platform. Fans add their own touch to popular tracks, while revenue flows back to artists and rights holders.
The feature, called Remix Lab, is available first only in France. The company plans to roll it out more widely soon, but for now it's accessed directly in the app through Deezer Club.

The feature runs as a remix contest. It can be found through Deezer Club or an artist's page in the app. Finished remixes can be streamed instantly, added to playlists and shared with the community — all only on Deezer.

Winners of the early-stage contest will be featured on a dedicated playlist of winning remixes, and will receive two tickets to Deezer's Purple Door event in September along with merchandise from the artist whose song they remixed.

Deezer has promoted better artist payouts. It says participating artists gave "explicit consent," and that any streams generated are fully attributed to the original work. "Every listen counts, and artists are compensated according to the rights they're owed," the company explains.

Deezer claims to be the first streaming platform to launch a remix feature with rights fully protected and agreed with artists. However, similar tools already exist — Spotify recently launched a remix tool together with Universal Music Group.

Spotify's remix feature also pays participating artists, but it uses generative AI to create remixes. Deezer's tool appears not to use AI, instead giving fans a tool to add effects and transformations themselves.

Deezer's head of product, Pierre Trochu, says, "This feature is focused on simplicity and accessibility. With just a few clicks, you can remake a song you already know and love — from simple effects like speeding it up or adding reverb, to sophisticated transformations that change the genre and style."

Deezer CEO Alexis Lanternier added, "This remix tool captures exactly our vision for products that enrich the listening experience, letting fans take part in the creative process and connect more deeply with the music they love."

'I'm not that interested in typing a prompt to make something. I'm drawn to breaking it apart and dissecting it.' That's what Jasper Shuoyang Zheng said introducing Latent Terrain, an intuitively and elegantly designed open-source Max external and UI that lets you play the unfamiliar world of neural audio codecs like an instrument, turning your own sounds into new textures.

It's a different breed from the hyped-up music AI making headlines. Here, the source of the data is the user's own sound. Processing runs on your own computer too, not a water-guzzling data center. Above all, it's beautiful and strange, and you can handle it directly through playing technique.
That's why musicians and experimenters are gathering around it. It turns the neural network back into a tool for discovering new sounds, rather than one that makes every sound the same.

Latent Terrain is a good place to start, especially for Max users already using FluCoMa or Data Knot. It generates a visual map like a warped texture, and you can navigate inside it however you like — with a mouse or a controller. You can also train a small neural network directly inside Max and watch as timbre breaks apart, splits, and melts into new material.
Keigo Yoshida's work is a good example for getting a sense of the sound. It's a piece that translates EEG readings into sound.

Beyond simple demos, there are artistic works that push the technology toward unpacking the meaning of sound. Jiatong Liu's nn/mémoire is a virtual gallery soundscape built from recorded sound of Beijing's hutong alleys. The rapidly disappearing sound world of the city becomes an ambient archive you wander through in space. Liu named 'learning to work with unpredictability' as a core design challenge rather than a problem to eliminate.

The documentation is excellent too. Jasper's own piece, 'Latent Terrain: Dissecting Neural Audio Codecs,' offers a good guide to the work and its possibilities. There's also a separate project page covering the research.

Example Max for Live devices are coming soon too, letting you choose from different audio autoencoders depending on the result. Several already-popular ones are supported. It's available to download for Max on macOS and Windows, and for Max for Live. The project will also be presented at NIME in London later this month.

Tidal said it will not monetize AI-generated content, shifting that responsibility toward distributors. Its position is that "the responsibility for identifying and tagging AI-generated content shouldn't fall on Tidal alone."

Starting in mid-July, it will begin identifying and tagging AI-made songs. At first it will only label music that is 100% AI-generated, with plans to expand the scope to works "substantially made with AI" as detection technology improves.

Its royalty policy is also clear. "Tidal's priority is to make sure royalties go to original works made, written and performed by humans," it said, adding that it will knowingly withhold royalties from music made entirely by AI.

AI music that exploits another creator's work, name or likeness will be blocked or removed. "We won't tolerate AI music that exploits an individual's or group's music, name or likeness, deceives listeners, or degrades the quality of the service," it said.

AI-made songs will continue to be allowed as long as they're properly labeled and meet the standards. The same standards apply to independent artists who upload their own songs directly as to existing distributors.
The industry is split. Bandcamp fully banned AI songs in January and iHeartRadio has also moved to ban them, while Spotify opened up generative AI features in partnership with Universal Music Group.

Tracktion's DAW Waveform got a major update, moving up to version 14. It adds features that help musicians and producers work more freely without hurting the software's performance. The core additions are a new LLM-based AI assistant, a redesigned GUI, multichannel audio routing, and expanded ARA2 support.

The AI assistant stays close to the DAW, offering context-aware help and creative support without taking your eyes off the music. It searches the software manual to answer questions, lays out multiple composition ideas or creates new MIDI sequences, and analyzes existing clips to write matching parts. It runs on a pay-as-you-go basis rather than a subscription.

The limitation of being tied to two channels has also been lifted. Input/output buses now handle multichannel audio, and the software can record or import multichannel files, with the tools needed for surround and spatial audio formats. ARA2 support has also expanded significantly — any ARA-compatible plugin can be used in time-stretch mode, and global and chord track information is passed directly to plugins.

The interface has also been smoothed out. The lower properties panel has been replaced with a new clip editor, making editing faster and more intuitive. The color scheme, icons and fonts have been refined, the title bar has been unified, and 18 colors can be assigned to taste. Also added: project management that drops legacy .tracktion files, DAWproject import/export for exchanging with other DAWs, and a raised plugin instance cap of 25.
It runs on Windows 10 and above and macOS 13 and above, with Linux support coming soon. It's available to buy now, priced from $249, with a 40% discount for a while to mark the June 29 launch.

The Atlantic has published four searchable databases as part of its 'AI Watchdog' project. Together they hold more than 20 million songs believed to have circulated around AI music generators such as Suno, Udio, and Google's Lyria. You can now check for free whether your name or band appears anywhere in this training data. At first it sounds like welcome news for transparency, but it is not quite as reassuring as it seems.

blocks.cap: AI training data 2026: The Atlantic reveals whose music went into Suno and Udio · Source: The Atlantic / Marcus Schmahl

blocks.x: The person behind this work is Alex Reisner. He has spent a while tracking AI training data for The Atlantic, previously covering books and research papers, and this time music. The result is four databases of varying sizes. The largest comes from the German nonprofit LAION, holding 12,320,916 songs scraped from YouTube — 91 years' worth of music. The second holds about 9 million songs, and the two smaller ones each hold around 100,000 songs. One of them was built on the Free Music Archive, started by the radio station WFMU.

There's an important caveat. Most of these datasets don't contain the audio files themselves, only links to YouTube or Spotify. Automated tools fetch the actual songs from those links, sometimes bypassing nearly every mechanism that sends money to artists, including logins and ads. Even so, there are still few lawsuits or clear rules to stop this kind of scraping.

What stands out about Reisner's work is that the search is completely free. There's no paywall. Just type in an artist's name. Berlin-based musician Heinbach says he found 151 of his own songs in a single dataset. Breakcore producer sophia_hjkl posted that 138 of their tracks were scattered across two datasets — by their own account, essentially their entire output from 2017 to 2024.

In June 2024, we covered major labels weighing lawsuits against Suno and Udio, which has since grown into a tangle of ongoing legal proceedings. At the time, the RIAA sued for massive copyright infringement on behalf of Universal Music Group, Sony Music, and Warner Music Group, and trade press puts the number of suits against the two companies at at least a dozen. Just weeks ago, Universal and Sony moved to add more than 61,000 recordings to their lawsuit against Suno. Warner has already settled with Suno outside of court, however, as has Universal with Udio.

Suno is defending itself with a fair-use argument, claiming that training generative models on copyrighted recordings qualifies as transformative use under 17 U.S.C. § 107. The central hearing in the case is set for July 2026, before Judge Denise Casper in federal court in Massachusetts. Udio, in filings from Sony's side, has acknowledged using publicly available audio for training while disputing that this amounts to infringement. Nothing has been decided yet.

In the end, all of this came to light only because four datasets were floating around publicly and researchers managed to get hold of them. Companies that kept their training sources entirely secret don't appear in this investigation at all, simply because no one could look inside. Reisner himself notes that this is only the tip of the iceberg. The first thing to do is clear: search for your own name or your band's name in Reisner's tool. It's free and takes less than a minute.

31 groups representing artists, songwriters, and their managers signed an open letter. They include the UK's FAC, Ivors Academy, and MMF. As record labels and music publishers begin striking licensing deals with AI companies, the letter calls on them to make several commitments to music creators, spanning creator consent, fair compensation, and contract transparency.

The letter was led by the European Music Managers Alliance (EMMA). Its CEO, Jess Partridge, says, "Amid this deluge of AI deals, EMMA has coordinated this letter out of growing concern over the land-grab on artist and songwriter rights." He adds that the way major music companies are pushing forward unilaterally in the AI space "is not the way to build a healthy, artist-centred music ecosystem," warning that "it risks repeating the mistakes of the past."

The letter starts by noting that labels and publishers, especially majors, are now "negotiating AI deals that will shape the future of music." These include the AI deals announced with Suno, Udio, KLAY, and Spotify. Even so, it says, "the artists and songwriters whose work, voice, performance, likeness and creative identity make those deals valuable are not being properly consulted." Some have begun receiving emails from labels and publishers that have struck AI deals, but the letter acknowledges this too often amounts to little more than "being told, by default and with no real choice, that they are automatically included in AI-related uses."

The broader fight over music rights and AI has always had two strands. First, on what AI companies owe, artists, songwriters, labels, and publishers are nearly unanimous: using existing music, or an artist's voice or likeness, requires permission first, through a licensing deal. Many AI companies argue that no permission is needed, citing copyright exceptions or the US fair-use doctrine, and the legal fight over that disagreement continues.

The second strand is a dispute inside the music industry itself: can labels and publishers unilaterally opt the catalogs they manage into the AI licensing deals they strike? And how is the money from those deals split among stakeholders? Majors have said they will seek artist consent for AI voice cloning and songwriter consent for AI remixes, but they do not seek blanket consent before licensing music for AI training. There is also little transparency about how the money gets divided.

The International Federation of the Phonographic Industry (IFPI) responded to the new open letter by focusing on the first strand. At a moment when "some tech companies, large and small, are effectively stealing almost every recorded song," it said, major labels "have sued infringers, pushed for legislation, and developed new licensing models to protect the interests of artists, songwriters, and rights holders, and to ensure they are paid." IFPI added, "we are strongest as a music community when we stand together." For now, though, IFPI is still sidestepping the second strand.

Formally endorsing the open letter, MMF chief executive Annabella Coldrick said, "On the question of AI licensing, artists, songwriters and managers have stood shoulder to shoulder with the wider music industry on the principle of consent." She added, "With this open letter, we are simply asking our label and publisher partners to extend us the same courtesy. This is not a right that is yours to sell." EMMA laid out three core demands: consent and control — no more automatic opt-ins; fair compensation — clarity on what percentage of revenue goes to creators, labels and publishers, and AI companies; and clarity and transparency — clear, accessible information in advance for any AI deal.
YMCK has released Magical FDS Plug, a free software synth that imitates the sound of the FDS sound chip.

blocks.cap: YMCK has released the free FDS sound chip synth Magical FDS Plug

blocks.x: For me, this is pure nostalgia. YMCK's Magical 8bit Plug was one of the first plugins I ever installed. I was deep into chiptune music at the time, and I ran it in MuLab, the first DAW I ever used. Writing that down makes me feel my age. Back then I was just getting into VST plugins, and after all this time, seeing a new release from the same developer feels a little strange.

There's another detail worth noting. YMCK's Yokemura says the plugin was built with help from AI tools. The FDS spec always felt too complex and too labor-intensive to turn into code, but recent AI tools finally helped push the project over the finish line. I wrote not long ago about a plugin made through vibe coding, and this is a good example of the hopeful side of that discussion. In the right hands, it could mean more good plugins actually reach us.

Magical FDS Plug recreates the sound architecture of the Famicom Disk System (FDS) sound chip. The original design is unusual: it uses a 64-sample waveform memory as the carrier, modulated by a separate 32-step instruction sequence. YMCK streamlined the editing flow to be more logical, letting you build the carrier waveform through additive synthesis, preset waveforms, pulse waveform editing, or free drawing across 64 points.

Additive mode works like a drawbar organ, blending harmonics with eight sliders. Preset waveforms include triangle, sawtooth, and sine, while pulse mode shapes a square wave using pulse width values from 1 to 63. The modulator section offers six presets: triangle, sawtooth, sine, square, ramp up, and ramp down. There's also a custom mode that lets you type a 32-step opcode sequence directly as text, using numbers from 0 to 7.

On top of that, it includes LFO, FM, and off modulation modes, ADSR envelopes for both the carrier and modulator, velocity and pitch bend support, and a switchable low-pass filter modeled on the original hardware's roughly 2kHz output filter. The interface is split into three sections: Global, Carrier, and Modulator.
