Global handles gain, polyphony, pitch bend range, theme, preset loading, and the hardware-style low-pass filter, while the lower half is where you shape the carrier waveform and modulation behavior.

Magical FDS Plug is open source, released under the GPLv3 license, with its source code posted on GitHub. The download also includes demo presets that keep the FDS parts of YMCK's demo songs intact. It runs as AU and VST3 on macOS 10.13 and up, and as VST3 on Windows.
AI-made music has quietly moved from a novelty into a real operational challenge.

Over the past year, the conversation around AI music has moved beyond questions of creativity or copyright. For streaming platforms, distributors, labels, publishers, and rights organizations, the more urgent concern turns out to be practical: how do you even tell whether a track was made by a human, by AI, or by some mix of both?

As the volume of AI music keeps growing, that question gets harder to ignore. According to figures from the streaming service Deezer, the platform now receives roughly 75,000 fully AI-generated tracks a day, a substantial share of all the music uploaded to the service.

This week, Boston-based audio intelligence company Modulate unveiled a new AI music detection API. Rather than relying only on metadata or creators' self-disclosure, the tool helps music platforms identify AI vocals and instrumentation directly from the audio file.

Many companies have so far leaned on transparency policies, under which artists, labels, or distributors disclose AI involvement themselves. But "there is a growing recognition that self-disclosure alone may not be enough." As AI music generation tools become easier for anyone to use, platforms are increasingly looking for ways to independently verify the tracks they receive.

Modulate says its system analyzes music by separating out vocals and instrumentation to look for signs of AI generation. Rather than a simple yes-or-no, it produces segment-by-segment verdicts. The company argues this level of granularity is needed as the industry moves away from the idea that every track can be neatly sorted into either human or AI.

The technology arrives amid growing concern over streaming fraud. Industry figures point out that AI tools have made it easier than ever to mass-produce tracks, which can then be uploaded and used for fraudulent streaming.

Of course, detection technology alone does not resolve every challenge AI poses for the music industry. Questions around copyright, attribution, licensing, and artist consent remain unsettled. Still, as AI music takes up a growing share of the ecosystem, many stakeholders have begun to see detection not as a peripheral feature but as foundational infrastructure.

For independent artists, the issue is less about whether AI should be allowed into music-making at all, and more about how to prove a genuine creator hasn't been drowned out in an increasingly crowded sea of synthetic tracks.

This is a video from YouTuber Songs by Spencer. True to its title, 'Suno Helped Me Write a BETTER Song,' he tests firsthand whether AI can really help write a better song. He starts with a simple acoustic demo.

He runs this demo through Suno AI. Rather than using the output as is, he treats it as a starting point for inspiration and remakes the song into a completely new version, layering human judgment on top of the AI's draft.
Throughout the video, he walks through how he uses AI music tools: sparking creative ideas, breaking through lyric writer's block, and raising the quality of songwriting and production.

This video is for anyone curious about AI, music, songwriting, or tools like Suno. It follows one creator's real workflow, bringing AI in as a songwriting partner while leaving the final polish to a human.
On Thursday, June 25, Suno launched a new artist incubator program called Spark. It gives selected independent artists grants and marketing support, and opens a path into Suno's songwriting camps.

Participating artists retain full creative control and commercial rights to their work. According to Suno, grant amounts vary depending on where an artist is in their career and can range from a few thousand dollars to tens of thousands. Marketing support is also tailored to each artist's needs, spanning influencer marketing and advertising, digital exposure, visual and art production, events and activations, and press opportunities.
Suno made clear it does not get involved in choosing or using a distributor. That decision is left entirely up to the artist.

"Emerging artists tell us the same thing again and again: tools alone aren't enough. They need support and exposure," Suno Chief Music Officer Paul Sinclair and Rosie Nguyen, head of creative economy and monetization, wrote in a blog post. "Spark's goal is to help more artists grow an idea into a finished project, connect that project with fans, and create new opportunities to build a career both on and off Suno."
Eligibility comes down to three conditions: being 18 or older, being a singer, songwriter, or producer releasing music under their own name, and being an independent artist.

Over the past year, Suno's songwriting camps have become a key channel for reaching music talent and introducing them to the generative AI product, which creates songs from scratch using nothing more than a simple text prompt. In January, the company invited Billboard to a private studio camp session in Los Angeles that included Timbaland, as well as Ommas Keith (Frank Ocean, Erykah Badu, Jay-Z) and Gino The Ghost (Sabrina Carpenter, The Chainsmokers, Saweetie). At the camp, experts used Suno to capture a song idea, then human musicians reworked the material piece by piece, adding their own improvisation and style.

On an episode of Billboard on the Record, Suno CEO Mikey Shulman was asked whether the company plans to become a record label. He answered: "No. We're thinking about building a music super app. A record label is a separate thing from that."

The program arrives just weeks after Suno announced a $400 million Series D round led by Bond Capital, which valued the company at $5.4 billion post-money. Separate from investor confidence, Suno continues to face copyright infringement claims from music industry incumbents.

Suno is currently facing a $500 million copyright infringement lawsuit from Universal Music Group and Sony Music. The major labels allege Suno trained on their copyrighted recordings without proper consent or authorization. (Warner Music Group was once part of the suit as well, but dropped out after settling and signing a licensing deal with Suno in late 2025.) German copyright group GEMA and Danish copyright group Koda are also each pursuing their own copyright infringement lawsuits against Suno.

This week, national class-action law firm Hagens Berman joined a lawsuit brought by independent artists who claim their copyrighted music was used to train Suno's models without authorization, infringing their copyrights.

Ableton has soft-launched Learn, a free music education platform. It opens lessons directly in the browser for people starting music and production from scratch, and there's a trick behind it: its interactive features run on the same engine used in Move and Note. Instead of embedding video, the lessons embed a simplified version of the Live clip view or audio, and the minimal screen strips away anything that might confuse beginners or kids.

It's still closer to a preview, and the early lessons target beginners. CDM's Peter Kirn sees that as actually important. It lets people clear the first barrier to entry, and "instead of prompting AI or something" — opens up a far more rewarding path to learning to make and play your own music.

What's up now is the 'Building Blocks' lessons and an intro-to-beats lesson. There's also something that wasn't in earlier online materials: 'Playground,' a radically simplified Live sketchpad for the browser. A few tracks made in it are up as well. It runs smoothly on both mobile and desktop, and Ableton told CDM it was built mobile-first.

Ableton's education projects have a long lineage: Dennis Desantis's book Making Music (2015), the interactive guide Learning Music (2017), translated into 19 languages, the free Making music at home (2020) released early in the COVID lockdowns, and tuning.ableton.com (2024), paired with Live 12's tuning system. When those projects began, Web Audio wasn't yet mature and Web Assembly hadn't arrived. Now that browsers can do far more, it's worth watching how Learn grows, and how artist involvement and use by education partners carry it forward.
Developer Pixelsncodes has released Lumen, a free, open-source Windows synth that turns images into sound. It's a wavetable synth built with the Claude AI coding agent.

The feature set is substantial. Two wavetable oscillators, each with Morph, Pan, Unison, Detune, Width, and Blend controls, are joined by a multi-wave sub oscillator, a multi-mode noise generator, and a state-variable filter with drive. There are also three ADSR envelopes, three drag-and-drop multi-wave LFOs, and a built-in multi-effects section combining Drive, Chorus, Delay, and Reverb.

The most unusual part is still the image-to-wavetable engine. Drag any image onto it and it reads that file's bytes and converts them into a wavetable. The idea of translating pixel brightness into sound isn't new — Serum and Ableton's Image2Wavetable Max for Live device have done it too — but it can be a fun way to shake up a sound at random.

The interface is split into two screens, Play and Deep. The Deep view gives access to everything above, while the Play view moves multiple parameters at once using just the image engine and four macros — Tone, Motion, Space, and Texture. There are 32 presets, split into Bass, Leads, Pads, Keys, and Textures.

For now it's available on GitHub as a VST3 and standalone format for Windows; a macOS version is in development. AI-made plugins won't be to everyone's taste, but releases built with AI coding agents keep increasing, with no sign of slowing down anytime soon.

Skrillex discussed AI and the humanity of art in his first formal interview in roughly a decade. It's a conversation in the latest issue of the Berlin culture magazine 032c, with his interlocutor British-Swedish artist Ecco2K. Born Sonny Moore, he said he'd been thinking about AI a few days earlier and something had struck him deeply: "I think the value of art can almost be measured by its ability to make someone feel seen."

"Maybe there are some AI songs that can go viral, but you can't have that feeling of being seen if there isn't a human on the other side." He said the reason revisiting Justice, Daft Punk, or Metallica hits so hard is that there's something familiar yet never heard before in them, and that feeling doesn't hold up if there's no human on the other side.

He also spent time on taking risks and embracing criticism. Saying he'd braced for pushback since his From First to Last days, he looked back on making tracks like 'Bangarang' with a Snowball mic or a laptop mic. "Starting from something imperfect forces you to end up somewhere you'd never expect." He also shared that his 2010 breakout EP 'Scary Monsters and Nice Sprites' came out on a marketing budget of $2,000.

The two-day event CONTRA, held in late May at Berlin's Kraftwerk, also came up. With Ecco2K, Bladee, Blawan, Knock2, and others on the bill, he said that the more we live in an age of AI and smartphones, the more important it becomes to create spaces where people can simply be together and feel together. Following June's surprise album 'SOMA,' this week he released the single 'Rumpta' with Solomun — part of the 'independent' chapter he's been in since leaving Atlantic Records.

Music data company Viberate has opened an official MCP server, letting AI services like Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, and Grok pull its data through everyday-language questions. Founded in Slovenia in 2015 and based in Ljubljana and Los Angeles, the analytics firm calls this launch the first step in its shift to being 'AI-first.'

The platform's data covers 11 million artists, 100 million tracks, 19 million playlists, 160,000 labels, and roughly 7,000 festivals. Through the MCP server, that data turns into artist forecasts, lineup suggestions, and marketing strategy inside a compatible AI assistant. MCP is the open standard Anthropic introduced and that OpenAI's ChatGPT, Google's Gemini, and xAI's Grok have since adopted — Viberate describes it as 'USB-C for AI.'

Co-founder and CCO Vasja Veber expects the entire business intelligence industry to eventually shift to a data layer that AI agents read and process. Where using Viberate used to mean two paths — the platform itself or the API — the MCP server is a third, and he predicts it will soon become the dominant way to use any data analytics service. "Anything they can do on the platform, they can do in their AI app ten times better and faster."

The company is also building standalone AI apps aimed at specific customer problems. Instead of crafting prompts, users just enter an artist, label, or track name, and the AI fills a set template with data from the Viberate API. It can also be fine-tuned on a client's own data, and it's currently in private beta for select customers.

Setting up the MCP connector is said to take just seconds. The free tier gives basic access, while paid plans unlock more than 20 advanced tools. For three months after launch, paid plans get a 20% 'founding discount,' locked in for as long as the subscription continues. Veber says AI integration puts music analytics at an 'adapt or die' crossroads, and he's confident that within a few years, more people will use the data inside AI services than on the company's own platform. "It's like having a consultant with the combined IQ of all the best data scientists in the world times a million."
Stretta, a synthesizer performer and developer, demonstrated Smol Sequencer, a browser-based modular sequencing environment, in a video.

The video shows the process of linking small sequencer modules together to build music patterns that keep evolving. It goes from tweaking note values and mixing in randomness, to learning scale-based composition through pitch-class rotation, to sharing your own musical ideas through a compressed, link-based project file.
Smol Sequencer is a free browser application you can start using right now.
Suno pushed back against demands from UMG and Sony. The two labels sought to add 61,000 tracks to their ongoing copyright lawsuit, and Suno countered by asking the court to block the move.
The issue at stake is fair use. This ruling on how far copying for training can be allowed could set a precedent for how AI music tools are legally trained and licensed.
So this fight isn't just between two companies. A line is about to be drawn here over which recordings can be used for AI training, and under what conditions.

Suno is preparing a developer API. Chief Product Officer Jack Brody announced the plan on LinkedIn, posting a link to an early-access sign-up form. The setup works like this: an outside app sends a text prompt, and Suno's generative model sends back finished audio. Instead of sending users to Suno, developers will be able to embed music generation directly inside their own products. Right now Suno has no official public API, only unofficial third-party wrappers floating around.

Brody stressed a cautious start. "We plan to start with a curated group of partners so we can develop this thoughtfully, and we're especially interested in applications that unlock experiences generative music makes possible for the first time." The Typeform sign-up form also says only that the company will reach out first to "a small group of folks," without giving a launch timeline. Brody spent 10 years running product at Snap before joining in late 2024, with former Warner Music executive Paul Sinclair and former Merlin CEO Jeremy Sirota coming on board around the same time.

The growth curve is steep. In June, Suno closed a Series D of more than $400 million at a post-money valuation of $5.4 billion. That's more than double the $2.45 billion valuation it had right after its November 2025 Series C ($250 million), in just half a year. Back in February, CEO Mikey Shulman said Suno had passed 2 million paying subscribers, $300 million in annual recurring revenue, and 100 million cumulative users.

The licensing picture is still only half-settled. Among the majors, the only deal in place is with Warner Music Group, which settled its lawsuit in November 2025; Universal and Sony remain in litigation. Last month, the two companies asked the court to add more than 61,000 recordings to that lawsuit. Last week, Suno also rolled out Spark, a support program for independent artists, which included a clause barring participants from publicly criticizing the company.

Klangio is a browser-based AI tool that turns audio recordings into sheet music, lead sheets and guitar tabs. You can upload a file, paste a YouTube, Instagram or TikTok link, or record straight from a microphone. Reviewer Ethan Hine tested it directly with several recordings.

Its strengths are clear. A cleanly recorded single acoustic instrument gets accurate pitch detection, ordinary pop vocals are tracked well, and chord recognition holds up. It offers Multi-Instrument, Single Instrument, Classical, Rock (beta) and Arrangement modes, and you can manually set key, tempo, instrument and time signature to refine the result. Output exports as MusicXML and MIDI.

The limits are just as clear. It wobbles on layered or processed sounds with multiple instruments, and misses the beat on swing, free expression or irregular rhythms. Drums, especially brushes or unconventional patterns, are weak, and it struggles with rhythms or tempo changes that fall off the grid. Old or noisy recordings are also tough for it. The built-in score editor is basic, so a proper polish still needs a separate program like MuseScore, Dorico or Finale.

The reviewer redefines the tool not as something that automatically churns out sheet music, but as something that gives you the cues to write your own score. It assumes a user with musical knowledge and editing skill, and the company's CEO said he doesn't expect AI to replace human transcription either. Pricing for Pro is £6.67 a month billed annually or £16.99 billed monthly, covering 50 transcriptions a month, with clips under 20 seconds free to use.

LANDR has unveiled the next phase of Fair Trade AI, its music licensing program for independent artists. This month it's paying participating artists their first settlement, while also launching a $1 million advance program that lets them take a lump sum upfront while keeping the recurring royalties still to come.

The program is open through July 20, 2026 to eligible LANDR Distribution users. LANDR Distribution is part of SOS For Artists and distributes music to more than 150 streaming platforms, including Spotify, Apple Music, Tidal, Amazon Music and Deezer.

Fair Trade AI licenses the music catalogs of artists who opt in to AI companies building audio technology, creative tools, voice apps and music AI. LANDR says transparent licensing is becoming increasingly important to the future of the music industry. Eligible artists draw from this $1 million fund to receive an advance that's settled against future licensing revenue.

Daniel Rowland, VP of Strategy and Partnerships, said that for independent artists, distribution shouldn't end the moment a song lands on streaming. He said the future of music distribution is helping creators find new revenue wherever value is created, that responsibly licensing music to AI is one of those avenues, and that LANDR already has the infrastructure to support it at scale.

LANDR raised the artist share from 20% to 25% of net licensing revenue. Artists are paid based on their contribution to the dataset, and additional revenue is added each time LANDR signs a new licensing deal.
BPB reader Wiseman has released WiseTracker, a free public beta tracker. It runs as a standalone Windows app alongside a VST3 instrument plugin called WiseTracks.

The backstory is fun. Wiseman isn't what you'd call a developer in the usual sense. But he's used trackers for decades, and lately wanted that FastTracker 2 feel inside a modern DAW. So he sat down with Claude and built it himself.

Yes, a vibe-coded plugin posted on a vibe-coded website. The same day we covered this, YMCK's Magical FDS plug was also a new music tool with AI's hand in it. This kind of thing has become ordinary now, and there seems to be no escaping the AI era for a while.

That doesn't mean it's a sloppy thing stamped out with a single prompt. Wiseman says he spent hundreds of hours designing, testing and rewriting it, and fixed bugs with help from Discord users. In the hands of someone who knows the workflow they want, AI becomes a way to bring into the world a tool that otherwise wouldn't exist.

WiseTracker follows the FastTracker 2 and Renoise-style workflow closely. You type notes and effect commands into a grid and move around quickly with the keyboard. It supports up to 64 tracks, 256 instruments, 128-voice polyphony, and 200 levels of undo.

Downloading it gets you both the VST3 plugin WiseTracks and the standalone app WiseTracker together. WiseTracks sits inside a DAW and locks to its transport and tempo, while WiseTracker runs without a DAW and has its own transport, tempo, metronome, tap tempo and audio device settings. The two share an engine, layout and file format, so an entire song, including patterns, samples, kits and settings, saves as a single .wise file. You can start in the standalone app and finish in a DAW, or go the other way.

It also works as a sampler. Drag in WAV, AIFF, FLAC or OGG files, map them onto the keyboard with the KEYZONES editor, slice loops by transient, tune by root note and pitch, and render a whole song out as WAV, FLAC or OGG. There's also a Euclidean-pattern-based rhythm generator for stamping a rhythm you like straight onto the grid. It can also import FastTracker 2's .xm and Amiga ProTracker's .mod files. It's free during the public beta and stays free after the full release under a PolyForm Shield license. It's Windows-only for now.
SpectraLayers 13 leads with AI processing to automatically split tangled audio into separate, independent layers.
The new Voice Enhance uses generative AI to reconstruct damaged voices, restoring speech muddled by noise or damage into something intelligible.
It's an update that could reshape workflows in editing, remixing and audio restoration.

zplane has released PEEL STEMS 2, a major overhaul of its real-time stem separation plugin, for macOS and Windows. Stem separation tools are everywhere these days, but PEEL STEMS takes a different approach: it runs right inside the DAW.
There's no need to upload audio to an online service or move files between apps; load the plugin and separate vocals, drums, bass and other elements right inside the session.

Version 2 focuses on making that workflow faster and cleaner. Updated real-time separation technology cuts latency at 44.1kHz from 483 milliseconds to 245 milliseconds. Intel Macs are still supported, with processing latency of 385 milliseconds on that platform.

Separation quality and clarity have also improved, with fewer artifacts than the first version. Real-time separation is most useful when it feels like an ordinary production tool rather than a separate cleanup step.

The Isolation slider now has a wider range, giving finer control over how aggressively a selected sound is separated. Spectral processing that targets specific frequencies and stereo zones is also included, which helps when pulling out only part of a sound instead of an entire stem. The Focus Frame in Focus EQ shows the upper and lower cutoff frequencies, and the interface has been refreshed with new visual feedback and stem colors.
All processing happens locally. That's useful when working with unreleased tracks or client material that shouldn't leave your computer.
It costs 59 euros, with existing PEEL STEMS users able to upgrade for 19 euros. A free demo is also planned. It's available as an AU, VST3 and AAX plugin for compatible DAWs on macOS and Windows.

Yamaha Music Innovations has updated its music-creation subscription service, Yamaha Creator Pass. The update widens DAW access and adds educational tutorials along with a low-cost tier for beginners.

The platform bundles creation, mastering, distribution and promotion tools from more than 20 partners under a single login and subscription. After debuting a public beta at SXSW in March, Yamaha refined it with artists to fit their production and release workflows.

The music tiers are now Starter, Grow and Pro. The new Starter tier costs $9.99 a month and targets first-time creators who want songwriting, beat-making and idea tools without any DAW, routing or audio-engineering experience.

Grow costs $19.99 a month and is aimed at users with some production experience. It includes Output Arcade, LANDR samples, a DAW bundle, plugins, LANDR's AI mastering, more than 200 online courses, and four Groover credits for pitching music to curators. Pro costs $39.99 a month and adds Output's Co-Producer, Portal, Thermal and more on top of Grow, along with 10 Groover credits.

Grow and Pro subscribers get Cubase 15 AI on both monthly and annual plans. Annual subscribers also get Ableton Live 12 Lite, and users without a DAW can download both at no extra cost. Yamaha said the service is designed to work alongside existing DAWs.
The first 100 people in the US to buy an annual Pro Pass by July 10 get a free Yamaha AG01 USB microphone while supplies last.
Remember Napster? Of course you do. The troublemaker of the early internet era is back, launching its own AI app and jumping into the AI music race.

It's a slightly different vibe from Suno or Udio. It's closer to an experience of hanging out with 'real' AI artists through chatbot characters. Napster CEO Edo Segal explained it this way in a Rolling Stone interview: "What we're trying to make is something closer to an experience. A human experience of interacting with another party, a back-and-forth creative process, like people jamming together to make something."

There's another interesting wrinkle. Segal said the new Napster app will license "ethically trained," copyright-friendly music generation models — the opposite of the days when fighting copyright law was the entire business model.

Napster has changed a lot in the meantime. Last year, the AI company Infinite Reality acquired the brand for $207 million. A $3 billion investment that was supposed to go into the relaunched brand fell through when the investor disappeared, and there are still claims that Napster owes roughly $9.2 million in royalties for streaming the Sony catalog even after the licensing deal ended last June.

Even so, the anti-music-industry stance hasn't changed. In Segal's words: "The major labels have been a problem that kept people from owning their own content and data, and that's still true. So we don't have much interest in building a relationship with them. We don't think labels are part of the future of music anymore."
"The old label model is dead. We've already seen distribution platforms like TikTok and Instagram spread and promote music far better than labels have in this digital era. I just think it's dead."

In Segal's view, Napster has always been on the consumer's side. "Looking back, Napster's core idea was this: you bought a CD with 27 songs from a store when you really wanted just one, ripped it to your computer, and wanted the right to share what you owned. I bought it, it's mine, so I felt I had the right to share it. Napster was an attempt to protect data. The core of our business is to genuinely protect and preserve data."

Asked how he plans to compete with Suno and Udio, which have struck deals with major labels, he dismissed those deals as "a very IBM move." "It's opened the door for major labels to figure out how to own the data, how to own all of this. That's the opposite of what we're trying to do. I want you — literally you — to own your own data and the content you create."
"I keep seeing attempts to bolt old business models onto something new, but the world doesn't work that way. You can't put a horse and carriage inside a car."
When the controversial AI-generated band The Velvet Sundown took off, TV writer and producer Simon Balch formed a counter tribute act staffed by real musicians: The Bootleg Velvet Sundown.

The Velvet Sundown became a sensation last year, drawing hundreds of thousands of monthly Spotify listeners. An unofficial spokesperson said the songs were made with the AI music platform Suno, but the band denied this, countering that they were a "multidisciplinary art project blending music, analog aesthetics, and speculative storytelling." Either way, it signaled that AI could now make genuinely popular music.

Now the pushback has begun. Balch wrote on Instagram, "What's the one thing AI music can't do? Play live." In other words, the one thing AI music can't do is perform live. He made clear that while he'd formed a tribute band for the most famous AI group, it wasn't a genuine tribute. "Instead of giving any money to the Velvet Sundown, I'm giving all the profits back to real musicians, whose work AI stole in the first place." In other words, the profits go not to Velvet Sundown but to the real musicians whose work AI took in the first place.

The group, made up of Leo Walrus, Enzo Allen, Milo Garland, and Luke McQueen, plans to re-record several Velvet Sundown songs in the studio. The goal is to rack up more streams than the originals. A tribute band has never out-streamed the act it's covering, so if it happens, it would be a first.

Some read the entire Velvet Sundown project as an elaborate stunt meant to expose the problems with AI music, while others see it as simple cynical money-making, given that it has already earned tens of thousands of dollars in royalties. Whatever the motive, this copy band carries itself with confidence. In a recent Instagram video, Balch narrates over footage of The Bootleg Velvet Sundown standing on a London rooftop: "If you're making AI music, be very afraid." It's a playful post, but real anger runs through it, and understandably so. "This is humans versus machines, and today, the humans are rising."
With the rise of AI, one little-noticed shift has emerged: the corporate hackathon is back. Musixmatch joined in too, inviting developers to build something with its own and partner APIs.
'Musicathon' was a global event held online for seven days in June. 523 developers built more than 100 AI tools and apps centered on lyrics, song metadata, and music search.
The three winning entries show what's possible right now. Fusion Karaoke reimagined karaoke by pairing synced lyrics with AI-generated visuals that react to the music.

Lyri is an "AI songwriting assistant" that helps break through creative blocks, drawing on Musixmatch's lyrics analysis and search API along with APIs from Cyanite, ElevenLabs, and Lalal.ai. SoundClash is a multiplayer music quiz game built for venues and classrooms, pairing Musixmatch's lyrics catalog with AI voice and audio recognition.

Sydney booking agency Good Intent has issued an apology after an AI-generated 'artist' turned up in a lineup they had put together. The show in question was the July 1 installment of Mixed Bag, a weekly new-talent series at Newtown's Bootleggers, which listed a name called Afro Charles alongside The Duke of Randwick, Pillar Lane and Genevieve.

Musician Aidan Sammut, who played the same show, exposed it the next day, July 2, in an Instagram video. He said another band member happened to look into Afro Charles's account and found that the visuals, as well as the music, lyrics and vocals, were "clearly and blatantly" AI-made. He pointed out that "at no point was it disclosed to us that we would be playing with an AI artist," noting there was no notice anywhere in the promotional material. He also called sharing a stage with technology that can only exist by stealing the work of human musicians on a massive scale "a complete insult."

Rob, who handles Mixed Bag at Good Intent, took full responsibility, saying he hadn't checked the artist's social accounts and believed it was a real artist because the booking agency had introduced it as a 'producer' who used 'live vocals.' Good Intent and Bootleggers said they have never knowingly booked AI music and never will, and promised to overhaul their vetting process and donate to the musician support organization Support Act.

The incident landed right as Australia's music industry is colliding head-on with AI. Last month, reports emerged that millions of Australian and New Zealand songs had gone into AI training datasets without consent, and this week artists and industry bodies including ARIA and APRA AMCOS gathered in Canberra to press the government for copyright protections. Sammut closed his video this way: "There is no place for generative AI slop in the live music scene."

iZotope has been acquired by VFX software company Boris FX. After Native Instruments was sold to inMusic last May, there was interest in what would happen to iZotope, which had been part of the same family, and it has now left the NI brand family for a new home. Existing licenses and subscriptions remain 'fully valid,' and support won't be interrupted. Account access and plugin purchases continue as before on the iZotope website, but purchases through Plugin Alliance are blocked for now.

It also closes the book on a tangled ownership structure. In 2021, iZotope and Native Instruments were brought together into a music tech group with investment from Francisco Partners, and in 2022 that group was renamed Soundwide and expanded to include Brainworx and Plugin Alliance. Then, in January of this year, Native Instruments entered preliminary insolvency proceedings, and when it was sold to inMusic in May 2026, iZotope was among the assets on that list.
iZotope's Todd Baker said, "There are no interruptions to plugin development," noting that the engineers who have built RX, Ozone, Neutron and Nectar are still on the job.

Boris FX founder and CEO Boris Yamnitsky named AI as the reason for the acquisition. "iZotope is known for its smart and practical use of AI," he said, adding that combining it with the AI audio and video technology Boris FX has built will let the company move faster and build more powerful tools. Boris FX is also the company behind pro audio tools like Sequoia, Samplitude and CrumplePop.

Finding music today is largely controlled by algorithmic curation on platforms like Spotify, TikTok, and YouTube. The new social platform Corus pushes back against this approach, putting human taste and personal recommendations ahead of machine learning.

Corus was created by Gabe Jacobs, a co-founder of Cymbal, a music platform that operated from 2015 to 2018. Corus is a social network for discovering music and movies together through recommendations and conversation. Early users include artists such as Nicki Nair, Daedelus, Conductah, and DJ Noir.

The app integrates with SoundCloud, Apple Music, Spotify, Tidal, and Deezer, letting people share across multiple streaming services. It works on mobile and desktop, and instead of Cymbal's Reddit-style recommendation voting, it borrows sensibilities from Instagram and Letterboxd to emphasize visual design and personal expression.

Jacobs describes the vision this way: "Corus... will be a place that connects and celebrates the art we love and share together. Social media today is painful to use, full of ads, bots, and algorithms that box us in. I want this to be different — more human, more genuine."

Pricing is split into free and paid tiers. Free users can post up to five times a day, while Premium, at $3.99 a month or $24.99 a year, offers unlimited posting, profile customization, playlist exporting, and a favorites-only feed.
Corus said it plans to keep running on subscriptions rather than ads. Going forward, it plans to add a trending conversation feed, spotlight features for new songs, and tools for artist monetization.
Starting July 1, music download platform Traxsource will add labels distinguishing human-made music from AI-assisted music.

The classification will be carried out with AI detection firms SH Labs and SoundPatrol. Tracks made entirely by AI from start to finish will be filtered out for removal, and the remaining music will be sorted into AI-assisted music and human-made music.

This step extends a position Traxsource announced last February. At the time, Traxsource said it would allow AI to be used as a production tool within a human-led creative process, but would not accept music made entirely by AI on the platform.

Co-founder and CEO Brian Tappert said, "We don't think AI is going away. Everything we do is about finding a way to live alongside AI while making sure the value stays where it should — with human-made work."

Co-founder and CTO Marc Pomeroy added, "We imagine a future where buying music becomes something like buying groceries today, with certified organic products sitting right next to regular ones, leaving the choice to the consumer."

With the labels in place, listeners can choose according to their own taste for AI. Traxsource will keep filtering out fully AI-made music every day, and it will also have a process for reviewing classifications if someone disputes them.
Sugarbytes has released a Claude extension for its drum computer. It's a free add-on that builds beats from a text prompt.

blocks.cap: The drum computer's Claude extension, which builds beats from text

blocks.x: A single prompt line is enough to complete an entire drum computer sound. You can see how it works in the demo video.
It's available now on Sugarbytes' website.
One user wrote in the comments, "Adding AI into the mix is aiding laziness, not adding efficiency or creativity," arguing that the existing random parameters already do the job.

RX10 arrived in late 2022, RX11 in mid-2024. In between, AI-based audio restoration and separation tools made a major leap forward, with competitors overtaking some of RX11's capabilities, and iZotope answered with RX12 after two years of research. Hugh Robjohns reviewed the Advanced edition in the July 2026 issue of Sound on Sound. New features grab the headlines, but it matters just as much that several tools have been completely rebuilt with machine learning and neural net technology.

The lineup is still the usual three: Elements, Standard, and Advanced. The flagship Advanced includes all 90-plus tools, plugins, and standalone processing features. Standard has more than 70, dropping the newest additions and most of the film and TV-specific modules, but keeping Dialogue Isolate. Elements is the entry-level edition with six basic noise-removal tools, and both lower editions can be upgraded to a higher one.

All three editions have a refined GUI that feels more modern, but the overall layout and workflow stay the same. The central spectrogram display is bigger, and a new monitor volume slider in the top right is especially handy when working on a laptop without an external interface. The rebuilt tools run faster and more precisely without losing audio quality. Pressing the new 'ear' button next to the preview button lets you hear what's being removed instead of the processed result — the so-called delta signal — making it easier to check whether the algorithm is throwing away anything important.

The biggest change is the 'Stem Split' button added to three stem-separation tools. It opens a 'Stems View' mode where, instead of separate tabs, the separated stems stack on top of each other within the same time-aligned spectrogram, a big workflow improvement over the previous approach. On top of that comes a new Scene Rebalance tool that brings what music stem separation has long done to movie sound, plus a search function that helps you find the processing module you want.
Apple has released Logic Pro 12.3. The update expands the stock plugins Sample Alchemy and Beat Breaker and overhauls the AI harmony analysis tool Chord ID, along with a pile of smaller improvements.

The biggest winner is Beat Breaker. The effect, which debuted in 2023 to slice and flip any source in real time to create glitch patterns, gains three new modes. Filter mode applies a low-pass or high-pass filter to each slice, letting you adjust filter type, cutoff, slope, and curve independently, while Resonance mode adjusts resonance per slice to create fast, rhythmic filter automation.
Pan mode sets the stereo position of each individual slice. Randomization controls that adjust probability and intensity are now available across all modes.

Sample Alchemy, which sits somewhere between a sampler and a synth, also got an update. The granular engine gains a new Sync mode that stacks multiple grain streams in parallel from different points in a sample, adjusting stream count, position, formant shift, and randomization. A new Granular Alchemy sound pack, showcasing the new mode with loops, one-shots, and field recordings, was released alongside it.

Chord ID, the AI analysis tool that picks out chord progressions in audio and MIDI regions, has improved accuracy on both single instruments and full mixes. Apple says it catches extended chords and inversions even when played on "an out-of-tune piano or a distorted electric guitar."

On top of that comes a new Producer Project that looks behind the scenes of Kehlani and Usher's 2026 track Shoulda Never, plus major improvements to Flex, the real-time time-stretching and pitch-correction engine.
Last week, The Atlantic's AI watchdog revealed that more than 12 million songs are being used illegally in AI development. Inside that "massive song dataset," SZA found 238 of her own tracks.

She posted a screenshot of the AI watchdog search on her private Instagram account, NotMusicAtAllISwear, and wrote: "if you're a musician and you support this depraved shit, you're disgusting, and there's nothing anyone can say to make this okay with me."
In a separate post, she singled out Diplo. "I don't know who needs to hear this but Diplo has a stake in Suno and is trying to train it on some of the best black writers/producers' brains."

Diplo praised AI on the Behind The Wall podcast last April, admitting he now prefers AI voices to real singers. "You don't need voices anymore. You can get the best voice from AI. You don't need anyone to sing for you anymore."

To SZA, training AI on Black musicians' work is just another way the music industry has diminished and exploited Black minds. "We are 13% of the US population yet influence the world with our sound and perspective. No protections in legislature, healthcare, or creativity. Easiest target to steal from... Do not train AI off your genius. Fuck these weird vulture ass men."

SZA's anger at AI has been simmering for a while. Last May, after guitarist Sophie Burrell called out an AI deepfake account that cloned her playing videos, SZA left this comment: "I genuinely feel so disrespected. It hurts worse that streaming services or labels don't protect or speak up for us. We are nothing to anyone."

MusicTech reviewed Fender's free DAW, Studio Pro 8.1. This version leans heavily on AI. The Moises engine handles both stem separation and stem generation, alongside vocal swapping and AI pitch correction.
The new beta feature “Studio Assistant” is an in-app chatbot that answers production-related questions. It's available at the Pro+ tier.

What stands out is a free DAW that weaves Moises-level AI directly into the mixing and mastering workflow rather than as a separate add-on. It changes what someone making music in their bedroom can do as soon as tomorrow.
Meaw Chain is an AI plugin that analyzes audio and builds a fitting effect chain using natural-language prompts.
Instead of adjusting plugins one by one by hand, it lets users describe the sound they want in words to build the processing chain, under a concept it calls “vibe mixing.”
IK Multimedia added eight Brazilian Portuguese voice models to its AI vocal synthesis platform, ReSing.
It's an AI vocal tool that turns guide vocals into a professional-grade finished take in a new language, and it arrives alongside the Singer Showcase platform, which scouts new artists.
TIDAL has begun flagging tracks it judges to be fully AI-made, and it also blocks those tracks from accruing royalties.
It's a policy meant to steer payouts toward music “made, written and performed by humans,” and it directly affects how AI music creators distribute tracks and get paid.
Image-Line's FL Studio 2026 ships with Gopher, an agentic AI assistant.
Gopher directly handles DAW functions such as track organization, mixer routing and piano roll content, so a single chat can get the work done.
As the first mainstream DAW to build conversational agent control into the creative workflow, it reads as a sign that how producers work with a DAW is about to change.
MotionTones is a standalone instrument and plugin that uses two-dimensional physics simulation as its composition engine.

Place a ball on screen and draw shapes, and the moment the ball collides, notes burst out from a scale or chord chosen in advance. Because the ball's motion keeps changing, the music keeps flowing and growing without stopping.
It supports MIDI input and output, so it can connect to other instruments or a DAW, making it useful as a hands-on generative composition sketch tool.

Audiotool 3.0 is out. It's a from-the-ground-up rebuild of the browser-based DAW known for its strong collaboration. Real-time multiplayer music making now runs in web browsers and on tablets, with a native mobile version coming soon.
This 3.0 release also brings Nexus. It's an open-source SDK that lets musicians and developers build their own instruments, plugins, and AI-connected creative tools directly into the platform.

Daniel Rowland, Audiotool co-founder and a producer himself, put it this way: "I've basically lived in a studio my whole life, and what held creativity back was almost never the person in the room—it was almost always the software. Audiotool 3.0 tears down that wall. Now anyone, anywhere, on any device, can create together, and we're opening up a path for people to build the tools tomorrow's music needs themselves."
Passing projects between producers has gotten easier year after year. Even so, work still crawls to a halt when devices don't match, plugins don't line up, or files go missing.

Audiotool says its newly built platform clears away these obstacles. The company says it enables real-time collaboration across nearly every device and has the lowest latency among online music production tools.

Beyond collaboration, 3.0 opens up the DAW itself through Nexus. Rather than relying solely on built-in features, users can build instruments, effects, visualizers, educational tools, music games, and even hardware-linked apps. The SDK also supports AI integration through MCP and Context I/O. Creators can connect whichever large language model (LLM) they want to the platform.

Andreas Jacobi, co-founder and CEO, put it this way: "It's basically Google Docs plus a creative sandbox like Fortnite or Minecraft. The DAW becomes a platform where creators build, experiment, and make music together." He said low-code and no-code development tools are bringing fresh perspectives on making music from people who never thought of themselves as developers. He added, "The next generation of music tools will be built by the people who actually make music."

Nexus's early partners include Splice, UJAM, BandM8, and Fraunhofer. Audiotool has also invited more music-tech companies to join. It's also launching its 'Let's Build!' hackathon series, running from now through August 23.

The history of music copyright is a record of labels and artists fighting endlessly. Over the past 100 years, the legal framework protecting artists' rights has been refined late, and unevenly, after each dispute broke out. A new front is opening now. Song generator companies are teaming up closely with labels over technology that existing authorship law doesn't handle well. The author, Hunter Hillman, is Head of Product at Daydream.

Even if every label licensed its catalog to Suno tomorrow, prompt-to-file generation would still hand users finished songs with unclear authorship. US case law and Copyright Office guidance hold that AI output made without meaningful human creative control isn't eligible for registration. Yet no one has actually defined what 'meaningful creative control' means, and Suno's product design doesn't encourage human authorship.

A flow where a single prompt goes in and a rendered file comes out leaves no trace of the choices a person makes along the way. There's no record of parameters changed mid-process, no discarded and re-recorded takes. That's why Suno transfers rights, title, and interest in the output to Pro and Premier subscribers while explicitly disclaiming any guarantee that copyright attaches to that output. After settling with Warner, Suno dropped the word 'own' from language that once said subscribers 'own' their songs, shifting instead to Suno technically remaining the 'author' while granting a perpetual commercial license.

This isn't a law of nature; it's a design choice. Picture the opposite case: if someone plays it like an instrument while sound keeps being generated, adjusting parameters in real time and recording their own performance, the human-authorship problem largely solves itself, because a person is visibly making decisions from start to finish. Prompt-to-file was simply a product built to create faster, demo faster, and monetize faster.

Labels still aren't backing down. Universal and Sony have kept suing instead of negotiating with Suno, expanding their case to cover more than 61,000 recordings, and Universal has licensed rival Udio while keeping its suit against Suno in place. Either way, artists are left out of the conversation. If AI-made music is going to properly claim ownership, the fix lies in tool design, not terms of service — building it so the person who made the work is unmistakably the author.
DJ and producer John Dahlback explained why he brought AI into his work. He said he especially enjoys using vocal-focused AI tools.

Dahlback has worked with Cazzette and Benny Benassi, and in his early days, under the name Johvan, he even made 'Don't Hold Back' with Avicii. In this interview, he said he treats AI 'like an instrument,' and finds it exciting rather than scary.

He told MusicRadar: 'I mostly turn to AI for inspiration. I use it as one instrument, like Splice or a synthesizer. Just as tweaking a synth here and there produces something, I use AI the same way. If you feed it a beat you're working on, it gives you ideas on where to take it.'

'When I was younger, I was deep into sampling. Rather than dropping a sample straight into the final version, I'd rebuild it myself and use that, and AI is the same for me. I'm also a firm believer in vocal conversion tools. I sing into the mic with my terrible voice, and it turns that into a polished singing voice.'
'If the person using it isn't lazy and is creative, AI is genuinely welcome. My older brother is an old-school producer who records bands the traditional way.'

'I used to be scared of AI in music, but my brother said it was amazing. A singer came in, recorded all the lead vocals, and left, and only afterward did they realize there were no backing vocals. So they fed that singer's a cappella into AI and pulled out great stems and backing vocals, making the vocals much richer. I thought that was a really great use of it.'

He also shared a recent conversation with the producer of a 'fairly famous Swedish singer' he couldn't name. That singer found a tape of themselves singing around age five, and there's now a plan in progress to train AI on that childhood voice so the singer can 'duet with themselves.' 'That's really amazing. I'm completely in favor of it.' Still, he drew a line at anyone lazily cranking out a pop song with AI and dropping it on Spotify, saying that doesn't make sense.

The RIAA and IFPI are leading an industry initiative to add standard AI labels to major streaming services including Spotify and Apple Music. The Recording Academy, SAG-AFTRA, the Human Artistry Campaign, and the American Association of Independent Music are also backing the proposal.

The labeling comes in two forms. 'AI-generated' applies to songs made entirely from a text prompt, or where machines created the lead vocals or main instruments. 'AI-assisted' refers to songs mainly made by humans that draw on AI for specific parts.

The labels appear as small tile-shaped icons. Fully generated content gets a white 'AI' on a black background, while assisted songs get a lowercase 'ai' on a white background, styled similarly to existing content-advisory labels.
RIAA Chairman Mitch Glazier said 'transparency is the best way to have it both ways,' pointing to both creative freedom and listeners' right to know.

A survey from Deezer and Ipsos found that 97% of listeners couldn't tell AI music apart from human-made music, but 80% wanted fully AI songs clearly labeled at the very least. However, this system excludes AI used in composition, lyrics, cover art, and music videos from labeling. DiMA, which represents streaming platforms, supports more trustworthy AI information flowing from creators to listeners, but hasn't yet confirmed whether its member companies will adopt the system.

Spotify and Universal Music Group recently previewed a paid AI feature. It would let Premium subscribers create covers and remixes using songs from participating artists and songwriters. Artists choose to opt in, receive credit, and get compensated. Universal called it the 'AI Superfan Initiative,' while Spotify said it opens up a new revenue stream and 'new ways to drive discovery.'

Spotify has spent years fighting fake streaming, because fake listeners pollute metrics, royalties, charts, and discovery. Yet now it's encouraging users to mass-produce synthetic versions of existing songs. The person pressing play might be real, but the music being consumed is itself artificial and derivative, and it favors catalog songs that were already doing well. It blocks one kind of AI distortion while turning the other into a revenue stream.

There's a difference between an artist using AI while making a song and a platform using a finished song as raw material for a new product. A song is a pile of countless decisions. Someone held onto a lyric they almost cut; someone chose the take where the voice cracked over the perfect one. Spotify is now trying to sell listeners a button that asks, 'That's fine, but what if you wanted something else?'

The discovery problem is worse. The songs best positioned for endless AI variations are the ones people already know — ones that already hold catalog value and attention. This isn't discovery, it's re-consumption. In a place where more than 100,000 new songs pour in every day, Spotify wants to pour in AI covers and remixes of familiar songs on top of that.

Participation should be voluntary, paid, and under the artist's control. That's the bare minimum to avoid theft, but a 'properly licensed bad idea' is still a bad idea. On top of that, consent gets complicated in an era when catalogs themselves get traded. As with the Red Hot Chili Peppers' recent sale of their recorded catalog, it isn't even clear who holds the right to approve and who can refuse. Spotify has already built the machine. Now it's a matter of watching which artists feed their songs into it.

BBC's head of music, Lorna Clarke, has laid out the broadcaster's music AI policy. BBC radio stations and its various platforms will always prioritize music that is the 'product of meaningful human creativity.' That doesn't mean creators can't use AI tools.

What the BBC does want is transparency about how AI was used in the music it plays and promotes. So artists and labels will be required to disclose their use of AI tools when they release music. At least in the short term, that won't be easy, since the industry itself hasn't yet decided how to identify, report, or label AI use in music creation.

Clarke also said the BBC 'won't knowingly broadcast AI-generated music that infringes on existing copyrighted work.' That, too, is a promise that's hard to keep. It depends on whether that means only music that blatantly infringes existing works in its output, or whether it also covers music made or touched by AI models trained on unlicensed music.

If it's the latter, the problem gets bigger. Most AI companies keep it very vague what existing content they trained their models on. Efforts like Ed Newton-Rex's Fairly Trained, which certifies models trained only on licensed content, help to some degree, but for now, there's a good chance that many of the AI tools creators use were trained on unlicensed work.

As a public broadcaster, the BBC always faces tougher scrutiny over its AI policies. Last year, 'BBC Introducing' West Midlands came under fire for featuring a mediocre AI-generated track in its artist-of-the-month segment, even though it seemed to be doing so to spark discussion about music AI tools on air.

In a blog post published yesterday, Clarke said artists who use AI tools will still be considered for airplay. But she drew a line: 'these tools should be used to support human creativity, not to replace the human role of developing, refining, and expressing the creative idea itself.' Simply entering a prompt, generating and picking a result, or lightly touching up an AI output isn't enough to count as meaningful human creativity.

This transparency policy grew out of listener research, which found that listeners care about musicians and human creativity and want to know how much AI was involved in the music they hear. So the BBC decided to require artists and partners submitting work to disclose whether and how they used AI.

This touches on a debate that's heating up across the music industry. Opinions differ on how useful automated tools for flagging AI music really are, especially for music that AI merely assisted rather than fully created. The industry still has no broad rules for self-reporting AI use, and those rules are now becoming urgent.

The way people discover music has completely changed. Fans, booking agents, even labels no longer just type an artist's name into a search box. They ask AI like ChatGPT, Claude, or Google Gemini questions like "who's an up-and-coming neo-soul artist in Roanoke, Virginia" or "recommend an indie rock band touring small venues in my area."

Asking fans to dig through social media isn't a bad idea. But if your online presence isn't tuned for both traditional search optimization and today's AI recommendation engines, you're letting new fans and ticket sales slip away.

The problem is that the algorithm knows you too well. Search your band's name from your own laptop or phone, and Google pulls in your search history, location, and cookies to give you a result tailored just for you. When your latest Spotify release and your website pop up at the top, it's easy to assume your search optimization is flawless. To see what a potential fan or a local booking agent actually sees, you need to strip away that bias. Opening an incognito window keeps the search engine from drawing on your past behavior, revealing your real, unprocessed exposure.

There are three things to check. See whether the top results lead to your official website and your current music service profiles, or whether they drift off to a dead MySpace page or a five-year-old local article, and fix the narrative accordingly. Both search and AI favor local context, so check whether your hometown, venue history, and local press are properly tied to your identity. AI models learn from structured data scattered across the web, and if you're not accurately represented on places like Google, Wikipedia, and MusicBrainz, AI won't recommend you.

The method is simple. Open an incognito window in Chrome, Safari, Edge, or Firefox, search your artist name, and see whether your active social accounts, Spotify, and website occupy the top spots. Also test local search with keywords pairing a genre and a city (for example, "Chicago indie pop band"). Then ask ChatGPT or Claude questions like "who is the musician [name]" or "recommend artists similar to [name]." Note any missing links, outdated photos, or incorrect genre descriptions, and fix your profiles, bio, and, above all, your metadata.

Managing your search exposure is no longer vanity — it's infrastructure for a modern music career. AI chatbots and location-based search algorithms are the new gatekeepers of fan discovery and local bookings. If you don't take charge of the data feeding into these engines yourself, you risk being invisible to a local booking agent or your next devoted fan altogether.
Italian DJ and producer Ciauru has won the Repli AI music contest, a competition for experiments spanning AI, music, and live performance.

He clinched the win after taking the stage at Kappa FuturFestival in Turin, alongside four other finalists chosen by an international jury. His winning piece, 'Raw Botanical Data,' used platforms like Krea (Krea.ai), SeeDance, and Higgsfield to turn video material into "impossible movement, recursive spatial structures, unstable textures."

Ciauru, whose real name is Simone Privitera, said: "Artificial intelligence isn't necessarily a threat or an obstacle. This time I used it creatively. Everything started in human hands, and those hands drove 90% of the work."

More than 1,400 entries were reportedly submitted to Repli for the contest. In that crowded field, it was ultimately a seasoned creator who rose to the top. Privitera has worked with well-known artists including Italian electro house heavyweight Benny Benassi, Dutch DJ Don Diablo, and American superproducer Steve Aoki.

Of course, many in the industry don't look kindly on his choice to dive headfirst into the contentious world of AI music. Jay Ahern, Chief Strategy Officer at the Association For Electronic Music (AFEM), recently warned of the risk of AI being used to "completely replicate someone else's creative work." The formation of the anti-AI band Bootleg Velvet Sundown shows just how far some artists are willing to go to protect live performers and reject AI in music.

"AI was a huge help in speeding up a process that would otherwise have taken much longer," Privitera said. "I hope more emerging artists take part. Building a connection with these platforms through efforts like this isn't just possible, it's extremely effective."
Techivation has released M-Compressor 2, an upgrade to its spectral compression plugin. Several things have noticeably changed.

The original's core features remain, combining upward compression, downward compression and gating. The Up, Down and Gate functions each have independent thresholds: signals above the Down threshold are reduced through standard downward compression, signals between the Up and Gate thresholds are boosted, and anything below the Gate threshold is attenuated.

As a spectral compressor, it applies different amounts of compression across frequency bands without splitting into multiple bands. Users can adjust the spectral parameters directly, or turn on the Shaping control, which continuously analyzes incoming audio and adjusts compression to prevent “muddy” or “harsh” sound.

The headline feature is the new Mix Assistant tool. It brings all of the plugin's parameters together into a single control. The tool analyzes the incoming audio and generates 12 compression settings tailored to the track. Users pick four of them and move smoothly between them to intuitively dial in the compression character they want.
It's compatible with Windows 7 or later and macOS 10.15 or later, and comes in VST, VST3, AU and AAX formats.
The introductory price is $55 through July 20, 2026, after which it rises to $149. It's available to buy right now.

Ocean Swift released DevOcean Modular, a software modular synth and sound design environment with 145 modules. What stands out is MaYa, a modular AI agent built in. It patches alongside the user, suggesting which modules to use and even helping wire up the connections itself.

This differs in kind from generators that turn text into a finished song. It is an early case of generative AI planted in the middle of a modular synth workflow to “patch alongside” the user, touching the very way sound gets made.
It is priced at 129.99 euros, 35% off the list price of 199 euros, with the discount running through September 1, 2026.
Eldoraudio has released "Guitar Audio to MIDI Converter," a browser tool that turns guitar recordings into standard MIDI files.

The guitar converter is a new addition to the existing "Piano Audio to MIDI Converter." Users upload an audio file and adjust the BPM if needed, and get back a MIDI transcription they can refine in a DAW.

It could help those who record guitar parts first and worry about MIDI later. Once a part is in MIDI, wrong notes can be fixed, timing tightened, tempo changed, or virtual instruments layered in, all without replaying the part from scratch.
It accepts common audio formats such as MP3, WAV, FLAC and M4A. Free users can convert the first 30 seconds of a file without signing up or registering a card.

Eldoraudio says the current model is tuned for clean guitar. It is optimized for steel-string, nylon-string, clean electric and jazz guitar recordings. A model dedicated to distorted and overdriven electric guitar is in the works. For now, the company says accuracy drops noticeably on distorted guitar.

The tool deliberately does not capture pitch bends. The company explains that models which attempt to track bends tend to handle them clumsily and throw off pitch, so it focuses on note accuracy and leaves bends to manual editing.

Because the output is a standard MIDI file, it can be imported into most DAWs, notation apps and tab tools. Native export to Guitar Pro and MusicXML isn't available yet, but the company says both are on the roadmap.

Although the model is tuned for solo guitar, it can also isolate guitar parts from mixed recordings and work on instruments such as harp, violin or piano. Still, for piano-focused recordings the dedicated piano converter works better.
The Eldoraudio platform also offers other audio conversion tools, including a stem splitter and a vocal remover. The guitar converter is the latest addition to that lineup.

Uploads are capped at 100MB, and paid plans support files up to 30 minutes long. Longer conversions are billed by the second at a flex rate of $0.25 per minute. Top-ups start at $5 for 20 minutes. A $15-a-month Pro plan provides 1,000 minutes of processing time and can be canceled anytime.
Eldoraudio said users may use the converted files commercially if they hold the rights to the uploaded audio.

BandLab Technologies, the company behind BandLab, Cakewalk, ReverbNation, and Airbit, has acquired Aiode. It's an AI studio that builds songs from fully licensed audio performed by professional session musicians and producers. It becomes the company's third production platform, after BandLab and Cakewalk.

Users start from a blank project or import their own audio, then choose a performer and style model to play on the track. Performances can be directed section by section, and pulling a new take for just one part leaves the rest of the song untouched. The finished result can be downloaded as stems or a mix.

The audio used to train Aiode's models, including the musicians' performances, is 100% licensed and traceable back to its source. After the acquisition, it remains a standalone product, and service for existing users continues without interruption.
Idan Dobrecki and Blue Dobrecky, who founded the company in 2022, continue to lead it as CEO and COO, respectively. Native audio recording and expanded DAW features are planned for a future version.
zplane has updated its real-time stem separation plugin Peel Stems to version 2. This release reworks speed, sound quality, and hands-on usability all at once.
The biggest change is latency. Processing latency at 44.1kHz, which was 483ms, dropped to 245ms — a 49% reduction. On Intel Macs, it runs at 385ms.

The separated sound also has less noise. The isolation slider now has a wider effective range, and Focus EQ raises both the upper and lower cutoff frequencies together. The GUI has been redrawn with a new stem color scheme.

zplane co-founder and CTO Tim Flohrer said, “With Peel Stems 2, we wanted to push real-time stem separation inside the DAW even further,” calling this version — which cuts latency sharply and raises sound quality — a major advance in stem separation technology.

In any DAW that accepts AU, VST3, or AAX, stems are split right there in place. It also includes spectral processing that narrows in on frequency and stereo range. All processing happens entirely locally, with no cloud upload, and it requires no subscription or login.
It supports Windows 10 and later and macOS 13 and later, and ships as VST3, AU, and AAX. It costs €59, with existing users able to upgrade for €19.

Spotify Premium users can now choose what to listen to by having a conversation with the app. It first opens on iOS and Android in the US, Ireland, and Sweden, for users 18 and older, and works in English only. Spotify says that since it's in beta, it won't always be smooth, but it plans to refine it based on feedback.
Spotify did not disclose in detail what technology runs underneath. It confirmed to TechCrunch that it uses a mix of its own models and models from several vendors, choosing whichever fits the task.

blocks.cap: You can now talk to Spotify

blocks.x: The scope of conversation extends beyond the existing AI DJ, letting users talk by typing or voice from the mobile home and playback screens. You can ask about a song's inspiration or an album's release date, or get other artists recommended based on what you're listening to right now. You can even ask about your own history, like when you first played a particular song.

You can say “play an artist I've never heard before,” then narrow it down by naming a specific artist or asking for recent songs. Saving a song, adding to the queue, and following an artist can all be done from within this same conversation. It is rolling out gradually to mobile in the eligible regions.

According to hacked data obtained by 404 Media, Suno appears to have scraped millions of songs, lyrics, and podcasts from YouTube Music, Deezer, Genius, and several stock music libraries. The material came from a hacker using the pseudonym Ellie.191, who hacked the source code in 2023 and 2024.

One file states that at least 2,013,545 music clips were taken from YouTube Music alone. A dataset list in another file shows 113,879 hours from YouTube Music, 62,117 hours from the stock library Pond5, 12,287 hours from Deezer, and 17,615 hours from Genius. The vocal model was trained on a capella versions from YouTube, and there are also traces of an attempt to download roughly 1 million hours of podcasts via PodcastIndex.

Launched in 2023, Suno has surpassed 2 million paying subscribers and raised more than $400 million at a $5.4 billion valuation. A copyright lawsuit filed in 2024 by major labels represented by the RIAA is still ongoing. Suno maintains that copying for training purposes is fair use, and CEO Mikey Shulman wrote, “learning is not infringing.”

In November 2025, Warner Music became the first of the three majors to sign a licensing deal and drop its lawsuit. This past February, artist groups launched the Say No To Suno campaign and issued an open letter.
Eldoraudio's browser-based tool converts guitar recordings into editable MIDI. Its distinguishing feature is the use of dedicated models tailored to the instrument's characteristics.
The first 30 seconds can be tried for free, and a dedicated model for distorted guitar is also in the works.
From playing a riff to refining it into MIDI, it removes the manual transcription step that used to sit in between.

Deezer said fully AI-made music has passed half of its daily uploads. Over June, that averaged about 90,000 tracks a day. It's the first case of a major platform where generative AI tools have overtaken human uploads.
Deezer is also working to filter out AI tracks tied to streaming manipulation or ones that haven't been played a single time in six months.
A market where AI churns out more than humans. Artists releasing music now have to compete inside it.

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is emerging as the AI era's “USB port.” It's a connection standard that lets music industry platforms plug their own catalogs and data directly into AI assistants like ChatGPT and Claude, pulling multiple tools together at once.
Creators and teams no longer have to open scattered tools one by one. They can now query several services at once, from a single place.
It's a signal of how AI music workflows can mesh together instead of staying isolated islands.
Suno released an iMessage keyboard extension. Without leaving the Messages app, iPhone users can make a roughly 30-second AI song using just a text or voice prompt.
A new Mashup feature that blends two songs into one was also added. Just pick any two tracks and combine them.
It brings the work of pulling a song out of a prompt right into the chat window people use every day.

ACE Studio 2 is an AI DAW built around vocal synthesis. It packs over 140 voices and 36 AI virtual instruments, plus generative tools like “Add a Layer” for layering and “Music Enhancer” for polishing tracks.

MusicTech's verdict is mixed. The next-generation AI features themselves are clearly powerful, but sluggish rendering and a rough workflow chip away at that strength. The tools have moved ahead, but the feel of actually handling them is still stuck in the past.

Project LYDIA, built jointly by Roland and Neutone, is a prototype-stage AI effects pedal. What sets it apart is that instead of just using a finished model, performers build their own AI model and play it live on stage in real time.

The core is an approach called “neural sampling.” It transfers one sound's timbre onto another, while still keeping the performer's dynamics and subtle nuance intact. Rather than locking the generative model inside the studio, it pulls it up onto the stage, changing how performers handle the technology itself.

Almudio released 3D Panner. It is a free early-access spatial audio plugin for macOS and Windows. Developer Almog built it over seven months as a graduation project at BIMM University Manchester, refining it through beta testing with instructors and students.

On AI, the developer said AI was used at certain stages of the coding process. He stressed that the DSP architecture, HRTF implementation, UX and parameter design were his own decisions, refined over months. In other words, it was not something thrown together.
The plugin uses binaural/HRTF processing to place mono or stereo sources in 3D space around the listener. It targets headphone mixing, ASMR, sound design, post-production, game audio and VR.

The feature set is dense. There's an XY pad for dragging a sphere around the head, an HRTF mode using HRTFs measured from 20 people and opening up the SADIE measurement database, and a Hard Pan mode for placing sources straight left or right. Frequency can be split into up to four bands with limiters on each, there are eight LFO motions — spiral, spring, X, pendulum, orbit, circle, infinity and random — and pendulum speed can even be set using the gravity of Earth, Moon, Mars, Jupiter or the Sun.

Install size is about 230 MB. It requires a free Almudio account verified by email, the license can be used on two computers, and a one-time internet activation is needed. It supports VST3, AU and standalone formats. macOS is Apple-signed, while Windows signing and AAX support are still in progress.
It is available for free at almudio.com/3d-panner.
Google has picked up the pace on embedding AI across digital experiences. This week, AI Mode search gained new integrations with Canva, YouTube Music and Instacart, rolling out gradually in the US.

On the music side, the core feature is YouTube Music. Users just ask in natural language for a playlist to be made. Tell it the genre and mood you want, and Gemini connects to YouTube Music to surface a recommended playlist right in the chat window, ready to play in the app.
The Canva integration generates design templates within AI Mode. Google cited a party flyer as an example, pulling in calendar event details to suggest a design that fits the occasion.
The Instacart feature lets users add groceries and ingredients to a cart within the app. It builds a shopping list by referencing saved calendar events like a barbecue.

Google said it is continuing to add more integration partners. The Personal Intelligence feature, which pulls in information from connected apps, launched earlier this year and has expanded its scope throughout 2026.

AI Mode has also recently added a Reddit integration for firsthand reviews, along with a redesigned intelligent search bar that lets users ask complex questions using video, images, files and even Chrome tabs.
In June 2026, AI-generated tracks made up more than half of Deezer's daily new uploads for the first time, about 90,000 tracks a day. That is sharply up from 75,000 in April.
Deezer said up to 85% of the streams coming from these tracks were manipulated. It is filtering out AI tracks used to inflate stream counts, as well as tracks with zero plays in six months.
It is a concrete figure showing how generative AI is reshaping what gets uploaded to streaming and how listeners encounter music.

iZotope is giving away VEA, a vocal correction plugin normally priced at $29. It compresses the AI processing from RX, Ozone, and Nectar into three knobs: Clean removes noise, Shape adjusts tone, and Boost brings out presence.
It targets podcasters, streamers, and producers who want RX-level cleanup without a complicated interface, lowering the barrier to machine-learning-based audio tools.
The free period runs through July 31, 2026, opening alongside Boris FX's acquisition of iZotope.
BandLab Technologies has acquired AI music studio Aiode. Aiode is a studio built on a fully licensed audio-to-audio model developed together with professional session musicians and producers.

With this acquisition, Aiode becomes the company's third music production platform after BandLab and Cakewalk. The key point is opening up consent-based generative tools to a broader base of creators.
German copyright body GEMA has officially launched PLAI, a music dataset and licensing system for AI developers. It covers roughly 180,000 recordings across more than 60 genres.
Rather than models trained on unauthorized scraping, it's infrastructure meant to support AI music generation that is legally clean and consent-based.
Developer and musician Matt Goodluck unveiled a new software instrument, Tonefield.

Goodluck said he drew inspiration from the now-unavailable old app Tonepad Pro. He said, “I rebuilt the concept from the ground up and expanded it into a modern instrument, releasing it as Tonefield.”
