Tonefield keeps the minimal, pattern-based workflow that made Tonepad addictive, while adding features such as selectable scales and modes, probability that evolves patterns, live performance recording, MIDI export, audio export, and pattern management.
Tap dots on the grid and hit play, and the music unfolds. Using the probability controls makes the pattern change every time the loop cycles.

The feature set includes the original Tonefield Classic sound engine with pure sine-wave synthesis and precise decay, a 16x16 step sequencer with an amber-dot interface, per-column probability, 13 scales including 7 modes and pentatonic variants, all 12 keys, BPM 40–180, velocity and gate controls, a delay with time, feedback, filter, and mix, and 8 named pattern save slots.

Live playing is recorded as WAV, capturing probability-driven variation in real time, and patterns can be exported as MIDI to any DAW, including Logic Pro and GarageBand. Audio is saved as WAV or MP3, and live MIDI is sent to the DAW while a pattern plays. There are also transformation tools like flip, rotate, shift, and randomize.
Tonefield is available now for $14.99.

Sony Music has sued the music AI company Udio again. After a bid to expand its existing lawsuit was blocked, it filed an entirely separate new complaint. More than 30,000 recordings are now at stake, and if Sony wins, statutory damages could exceed $4.5 billion.

Judge Alvin K Hellerstein ruled that expanding the complaint now would “substantially prejudice” Udio. But he added that Sony could enforce its rights over every recording it claims was infringed, and nothing required it to do so in this lawsuit. Sony read that line as permission to sue separately.

Two years ago, Sony sued Udio alongside Universal Music and Warner Music. Both of those labels later settled and signed licensing deals. Only 333 recordings were named in the first lawsuit; the remaining 30,000-plus have now surfaced in this one.

The new complaint makes three arguments. Udio scraped recordings from YouTube through “illegal ‘stream ripping.’” AI-generated music floods the market and cheapens music made by humans. And fair use does not apply. As a final point, Sony wrote that what Udio produces is machine-imitated music, not human creation.
Sony is using Universal’s and Warner’s licensing deals as leverage. The logic: an AI music licensing market is already running, which means Udio itself has effectively admitted it needs permission.
Google has expanded the Flow Music platform, adding song generation, editing, and stem separation to Spaces, its “vibe coding” tool.
Musicians can now make a song, swap out a specific verse, separate vocals, extend a track, and pull out album art, lyrics, and video, all within a single workspace.
All of this runs on Lyria 3 Pro layered with Gemini, Veo, and Nano Banana.
MusicTech tested nine leading AI stem-separation tools, and performance varied widely by song and instrument.
Logic Pro led on fast, everyday separation, while MVSEP had the edge on difficult vocals and the hardest-to-isolate parts.
As of 2026, it serves as a practical map of where neural source separation actually helps producers.
Team Exile has previewed Karst, a digital modular environment that makes music through systems and algorithmic composition.
It comes with a node editor, cableless patching, and cloud sync. Every instrument carries an event core.
Thanks to the event core, you can hand-write generative algorithms directly, without wrestling with event scheduling or polyphony.
Google has tuned its AI music generation model and released Lyria 3.5 inside Flow Music. It's an upgrade aimed squarely at Suno.
DeepMind says the new model is markedly better across musicality, lyrics and vocal quality overall. Vocals sound more realistic with real emotional texture, and diction is noticeably clearer.
Melodic structure is also richer and more natural, raising the bar for vocal quality that producers will face starting tomorrow.
Tunery Instruments has released Silt, a “generative tape loop instrument.”
Four short melodic loops of different lengths pass through an emulated tape machine, slowly drifting out of phase.
That produces an ever-shifting ambient pattern, built for producers chasing vintage warmth.
Vochlea's new app, Dubbox, uses machine learning to turn beatboxing into real-time, sample-based drum loops.
The app learns up to eight of a user's vocal hits, then triggers drum samples that respond to velocity.
The “Voice Warping” feature snaps a played take to the grid while keeping the feel of the original performance.

Epidemic Sound announced a partnership with Overwolf and MyPart to launch a new Stream mode in Songhunt, the Overwolf in-game app that gives PC gamers a personalized, adaptive music experience across more than 1,500 PC games.

Songhunt uses MyPart's multimodal AI to interpret gameplay continuously and select music from Epidemic Sound's catalog that matches what is happening on screen, shifting from quiet exploration to fast-paced combat.

For streamers on Twitch and YouTube, Epidemic Sound's 100% IP-owned catalog removes the risk of muted VODs, copyright claims and takedowns. "Songhunt removes that trade-off," said Rasmus Thofte, SVP B2B at Epidemic Sound.
On the latest episode of Las Culturistas, Kelly Clarkson said a lot of good can come from AI: "Controversial? I don't care: I love AI. ... I'm into it artistically, too. I have fun with it."
She called most opinions on AI music too "black-and-white": "I think it's welcome to the table ... but I don't think they should be competing with humans."
"When you see AI artists competing on a chart with humans, I have an issue," she said. "I think there should be a separate chart ... We can't lose human."
In August, Billboard reaffirmed its commitment to transparently note when an AI-generated song enters its charts, as Luminate announced plans to label AI-created content.

Shoegaze outfit SLEEP CLUB's latest single "Weight Of Ease", from their upcoming debut album "Dweller", has seemingly been incorrectly flagged by Spotify for AI usage. The band's entire catalog had previously been flagged before Spotify resolved it.

"For the 2nd time in two releases, our newest single 'Weight of Ease' has been flagged by Spotify's AI driven internal system as 'ineligible for recommendation'," said Matt Jones, noting algorithmic support makes up roughly 50-70% of an average artist's streams. It took roughly 5 weeks to restore the catalog.

"It's ironic that this album, which is about the intrusion of AI into every aspect of our lives, keeps getting flagged by AI systems incorrectly," he added. The band later said the first flag stemmed from the word "sleep" in their name; Spotify has not explained the current one.

AWS walks through deploying a music production pipeline on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime Instances, managed EC2 infrastructure that adds multi-day sessions, GPUs, persistent volumes and colocation of multiple agents.

blocks.cap: The three-agent pipeline (Compose, Deliver, Screen) sharing one GPU instance and session

blocks.x: A composition agent turns a producer's request into a brief with Claude Sonnet 4.6 and renders audio with the open-source ACE-Step model on the instance's NVIDIA L4 — 20 seconds of 48 kHz stereo in about 9 seconds. A delivery agent measures the .wav and applies an EQ, compression and limiting chain; a compliance agent re-measures it and screens it against the studio's back catalog, asking for a replacement if it flags a match.
Invoked with the same session ID, the agents share one instance and filesystem, and sessions can persist for up to 14 days.

Todd Edwards, a house and UK garage legend and master of sampling, sat down for a long conversation with MusicRadar. He covered his 34-year career, his first UK show, his repeated collaborations with Daft Punk, and his thoughts on today's DJ culture.

His first piece of gear was an Ensoniq EPS sampling workstation. Its signature 13-bit grit and famous swing both came from there. With no keyboard at the time, he stitched together hundreds of short samples to build music and lyrics. He recalls that he "treated records like paint, like raw material."

With hundreds of micro samples in a single track, clearing each one individually is close to impossible. As AI made it easier to detect samples and copyright lawsuits grew more common, he had to change his approach. In early 2025 he tried playing synths or making his own samples with Splice, but he missed the joy of digging through records, and it left him depressed.

The breakthrough was the AI music platform Suno Studio. Making material he could safely sample there brought back the joy of making music. "I hate it when people talk about this technology like it came from the devil," he says. He adds that seasoned producers see it as a powerful tool, while those without skills see it as a threat.

He believes making stems with AI to sample is no less creative than picking a Splice loop. That's also where he says "the hypocrisy in the industry is remarkable." A plain prompt alone produces something generic, he says, but if he puts in his own ideas to make a disco or soft rock track and then cuts it up, "it's all mine, so I never have to worry about a lawsuit again."
Having made music his whole life without AI, he says he uses it because "it's an amazing adventure," adding that in the end it comes down to how you use it.
